_README: Approach variants — MOUNT RAINIER and the SOUTHERN WASHINGTON volcanoes and ranges, 2026-08-19.
42 routes, 42 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
`area` on every entry was READ FROM THE LIVE ROW (routes.area_id), not typed from the route name. That matters
more here than in most batches, because SIX ids in this scope carry no peak name at all — wa_bread_loaf,
wa_scramble_route, wa_southwest_scramble, wa_east_ridge_8, wa_the_roof, wa_open_book_2, wa_fantasy_falls — and
TWO DIFFERENT ROUTES IN THIS BATCH ARE BOTH CALLED 'Classic Route': wa_classic_route_2 is on UNICORN PEAK and
wa_classic_route_3 is on LANE PEAK, four miles apart in the Tatoosh. A name-shaped id is not evidence of which
peak you are on, and here it is not even evidence of which climb.
SCOPE WALKED: wa_mount_rainier, wa_liberty_cap, wa_point_success, wa_little_tahoma (all under
usa.washington.wa_sw_tacoma.wa_southwest_cascades), wa_mount_adams, wa_mount_st_helens, the Goat Rocks peaks
(wa_gilbert_peak, wa_ives_peak, wa_old_snowy_mountain) and the six Tatoosh Range peaks the catalog holds
(wa_castle_peak_tatoosh, wa_eagle_peak, wa_lane_peak, wa_pinnacle_peak_tatoosh, wa_plummer_peak,
wa_unicorn_peak). 59 routes in those areas; 13 already carried approach_variants and were NOT touched;
46 were empty. 42 are written here and 4 were deliberately skipped — see _SKIPPED.
FOUR REQUESTED PLACES DO NOT EXIST IN THE CATALOG and so could not be covered: MOUNT AIX, AMERICAN RIDGE,
DENMAN PEAK and CHUTLA PEAK, plus WAHPENAYO PEAK. None has an area row, under any spelling, anywhere in the
Washington tree. Denman and Chutla are named in the prose of routes written here (Denman as the peak on the
far side of the Lane-Denman saddle, and as the wrong fork at Plummer's tarn) but neither carries a row of its
own. Note also that 'Curtis Gilbert' in the request is wa_gilbert_peak — Mount Curtis Gilbert and Gilbert Peak
are the same 8,184 ft Goat Rocks summit, one row, and it is covered. There is no separate Curtis Gilbert row.
TWO STRUCTURAL SETS IN THIS BATCH ARE THE COLFAX SHAPE — several lines off one bench, told apart by a test
that works ABOVE the schrund plus a negative test — and they were written as sets rather than individually:
- LANE PEAK'S NORTH FACE: three couloirs (LOVER'S LANE, THE ZIPPER, THE FLY, left to right) dropping onto one
debris apron. Told apart by WIDTH (the Zipper narrows 40 ft to 20 ft; the Fly stays 40-50 ft), by a COUNT OF
STEPS (the Zipper has up to three; the Fly has none), by ANGLE (Lover's Lane reaches ~60 degrees, the others
~45), and definitively by WHERE THEY TOP OUT (the Zipper at a dead tree in an east-ridge notch, the Fly at
the west-ridge notch, Lover's Lane on the ridge ABOVE the Zipper — from which the standard descent rappels
INTO the Zipper, so being able to look down into a neighbouring couloir is the confirmation).
- UNICORN PEAK'S SUMMIT HORN: three lines within about 70 ft (THE ROOF, CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK, left to
right) that all finish at the same slung block. Told apart at the ground by TACTILE tests: a roof overhead
and a chimney is The Roof; blocky open face with a piton at half height is the Classic Route; two wide
left-leaning cracks that want big cams is Open Book. The left-to-right ordering is re-homed from the rows'
own prose ('about 20 ft left of the Classic Route where the ridgeline meets the block' and 'about 50 ft
right of the base of the Classic Route'), not inferred.
- A THIRD SET IS RAINIER'S MOWICH FACE, and it is the same problem at a much larger scale: four climbs share
one camp and one walk-in. They are separated by WHICH GLACIER you cross from the divide bivy and by WHERE
THE HOURGLASS IS — the North Mowich Headwall's is in the first 50 ft, the Central Mowich Face's is at
12,500 ft, and the Edmunds Headwall's schrund is turned beside TWIN GENDARMES.
- AND A FOURTH, SMALLER: the FUHRER THUMB, which is the middle of three features seen from the upper Wilson
Glacier — WILSON GLACIER HEADWALL, FUHRER THUMB, FUHRER FINGER, left to right. The Thumb is the narrow one;
the Finger is the wide one with the hourglass. They merge at ~11,500 ft, so a misidentification cannot be
detected above that height and must be settled at the bottom.
RAINIER'S TRAILHEADS ARE THE OTHER STRUCTURAL PROBLEM, and every Rainier baseFinding names its side of the
mountain because a party at the wrong one is hours away. The routes written here leave from FIVE different
roadheads: PARADISE (Nisqually Icefall, Fuhrer Thumb, Kautz Headwall, Little Tahoma's Cowlitz/Ingraham line),
WHITE RIVER (Curtis Ridge, Willis Wall), FRYINGPAN CREEK on the Sunrise road (Little Tahoma's standard),
MOWICH LAKE (Mowich Face, North Mowich Headwall, Central Mowich Face, Edmunds Headwall) and WESTSIDE ROAD
(Sunset Ridge, Tahoma Glacier). Where routes share a camp the finding is which side of it they leave from:
the Mowich lines all DESCEND off the Ptarmigan Ridge camp rather than climbing from it, and the Little Tahoma
winter line leaves the Camp Muir track at 8,600 ft — 1,500 ft BELOW Camp Muir, so reaching that camp means
you have overshot.
LIVE CLOSURES WERE NOT WRITTEN AS DURABLE DATA. Several rows in this scope store dated closure claims in their
own columns (see _DEFECTS). What is written here instead is the durable pattern: Mowich Lake Road is unpaved
and typically opens well after the east- and south-side roads, commonly not until July, and closes with the
first significant snow; highway access to it from the north has been interrupted for extended periods and
should be confirmed rather than assumed in either direction. Westside Road is gated to vehicles a few miles in
because of repeated Tahoma Creek flooding and the remainder is walked or biked. Stevens Canyon Road is gated
roughly mid-October to late May. No year is named anywhere in a variant.
Contamination rejected during research, recorded so it is not re-introduced:
- MOUNT ADAMS. There is a Mount Adams in New Hampshire's Presidential Range (5,799 ft, and the second-highest
peak in the northeastern US, so it dominates a plain name search) and further Mount Adams summits elsewhere.
Every Adams source used here is anchored to Killen Creek, Takhlakh Lake, the High Camp Trail, Cold Springs,
Trout Lake or the Round the Mountain Trail, none of which any other Mount Adams has.
- LYMAN GLACIER. There are TWO Lyman Glaciers in Washington: the one on Mount Adams used here, and a much
better-documented one at Lyman Lake in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, about 100 miles north. Searches return
the northern one first. Nothing from Lyman Lake, Spider Gap or Railroad Creek was used for any field.
- PINNACLE PEAK. The one here is the 6,562 ft Tatoosh peak above Reflection Lakes. It is distinct from
wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat (a Sawtooth/Chelan peak), from the Enumclaw 'Pinnacle Peak' / Mount Peak, and
from wa_central_pinnacle, wa_nw_pinnacle, wa_sw_pinnacle and wa_south_central_pinnacle, which are crags in
the Chimney Rocks group near the Columbia Gorge and are in a different subtree entirely.
- THE CASTLE. wa_castle_peak_tatoosh is NOT wa_castle_peak_pasayten, a peak of the same name 150 miles north
in the Pasayten with four routes of its own. Nor is it any of the three Castle Rocks in the catalog
(Tumwater Canyon x2, Glacier Peak Wilderness). Only Reflection Lakes / Pinnacle Saddle material was used.
- SNOW LAKE and BENCH LAKE. The Unicorn Peak approach uses the Snow Lake in Mount Rainier National Park, on
Stevens Canyon Road. Washington's famous Snow Lake is at Snoqualmie Pass, 60 miles north, and there is a
Bench Lake beside it. Nothing from the Snoqualmie lakes was used.
- EAGLE PEAK. The Tatoosh Eagle Peak above Longmire is one of many Eagle Peaks and Eagle Rocks in the
catalog (wa_eagle_rock in the Stevens Pass region, wa_eagle_rock_a_k_a_school_rock in the Olympics,
wa_bald_eagle_peak in the western Alpine Lakes). Only Longmire / Nisqually suspension bridge material was
used.
- GOAT MOUNTAIN vs the GOAT ROCKS. 'Goat' names a great deal of Washington. The Goat Ledges, Goat Ribs and
Goat Creek used here are all in the Goat Rocks Wilderness on the Snowgrass Flat side; nothing was carried
from Goat Mountain on the Mount Baker Highway, which another batch covers.
- OLD SNOWY. Distinct from Snowy Mountain in the Pasayten. Only Snowgrass Flat / PCT material was used.
- 'TAHOMA'. Tahoma is a name for Mount Rainier itself, and the catalog also holds a Tahoma Glacier route ON
Rainier and a separate peak, LITTLE TAHOMA. wa_mount_rainier_tahoma_glacier and the three wa_little_tahoma
routes are different mountains' worth of ground and were kept strictly apart.
- CURTIS. Curtis Ridge is on Rainier's north side; Mount Curtis Gilbert is in the Goat Rocks; there is also a
Curtis Glacier on Shuksan and a Camp Curtis on Rainier's Emmons side. Only the Winthrop-Glacier-side
material was used for Curtis Ridge.
No time, distance or gain figure is averaged. Where two sources disagreed, the field is omitted. Several
variants deliberately carry no hours at all.
_confidence values used here: 'corroborated' (two or more independent published sources agree on the base),
'thin' (the base is real but under-published, and the variant says so), and 're-homed' (the material comes
from the route row's OWN approach / beta / descent_text / pitch_detail / climbing_route columns and no
external source was captured for it — nothing was researched into these, and _sources is empty by design).
Most of the Tatoosh and Goat Rocks entries are re-homed: those rows are unusually rich, and the base findings
in them are re-organisations of facts the rows already held, not new research.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Skyline Trail and the Nisqually Glacier to the lower bergschrund
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun. This is an early-season line: the icefall wants to be frozen, and hazard rises steeply through the summer as the glacier warms
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise at about 5,400 ft, follow the Skyline Trail up past Glacier Vista and Pan Point, then leave it and drop west onto the Nisqually Glacier. This is the same access point the Wapowety Cleaver lines use. Rope up before you step onto ice; there is no maintained trail from here on and no reliable water once you leave Paradise, so plan on melting snow.

Ascend the Nisqually alongside the Wapowety Cleaver, gaining steadily to about 9,900 ft where the lower bergschrund marks the start of the technical ground — typically 40 to 50 ft of steep ice or snow to gain the icefall itself.

Above that the route threads broken, crevassed terrain in the upper Nisqually basin toward the top of the Wapowety Cleaver near 13,000 ft. That basin is the most time-consuming and the most dangerous section of the whole climb: it sits directly under active icefall and rockfall, and the correct tactic is to move through it without stopping to regroup. The seracs rearrange themselves every season, so expect to find your own way rather than follow anyone's line.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIMBING STARTS AT THE LOWER BERGSCHRUND AT ABOUT 9,900 FT. Everything below that is glacier walking, and the whole recognition problem is not confusing that walking with progress.

FIRST TEST, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES THE DAY: which way you go at Glacier Vista. This route drops WEST off the Skyline Trail onto the Nisqually. If you are still walking uphill on maintained trail toward Pebble Creek and the Muir Snowfield, you are on the Camp Muir approach and the icefall is behind your left shoulder. Parties have made that mistake in the dark because the first mile is identical.

SECOND TEST, AND IT WORKS IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT IS A SIDE, NOT A LANDMARK: the Wapowety Cleaver — the rock cleaver dividing the Nisqually from the Kautz — must stay on your LEFT the whole way up. If it has ended up on your right you have crossed onto the Kautz side of it and you are on the Kautz Glacier route.

THIRD TEST, POSITIVE: the schrund is the first steep ground on the route. If you have walked moderate glacier for hours and met nothing steeper than a crevasse crossing, you have not arrived — keep going, do not start climbing something because it is steep.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE MOST USEFUL ONE HERE, AND IT INVERTS THE USUAL INSTINCT: a boot track is EVIDENCE YOU ARE WRONG. This route is circuitous enough and dangerous enough that it is rarely climbed in any given season. A trench underfoot on the Nisqually almost certainly belongs to parties walking to Camp Muir, not to anyone on this line.

WHAT BEING TOO HIGH LOOKS LIKE: if you are in the upper basin with seracs above you and have not crossed a bergschrund, you have wandered into the icefall from the side rather than climbing into it, which is exactly the ground you least want to be standing still in.
hazards: Active icefall with collapsing seracs directly above the upper basin
Complex crevasse and serac navigation that changes every season
Hazard rises rapidly with warming through the day, so the upper basin must be crossed early
Documented history of large slide activity in the icefall
No reliable water above Paradise

approach_variants.name: White River, Glacier Basin, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop Glacier traverse
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun, in cold stable conditions when the rock is frozen in place
approach_variants.notes:
From White River Campground, hike the Glacier Basin Trail about 3.5 miles and 1,700 ft to Glacier Basin near 5,900 ft — a broad basin with the last reliable running water and a common camp. Continue on climbers' path up to St Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, another 1,500 ft over roughly a mile of steepening scree and snow.

At the pass, rope up. Drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour west and southwest between roughly 7,200 and 7,400 ft, threading crevasses, to reach the base of Curtis Ridge on its east side.

This is the same corridor Liberty Ridge parties use, so in season there is often a boot track and other parties on it. Above St Elmo Pass there is no water at all.

Rockfall on the traverse concentrates in three places: immediately after you drop onto the glacier, roughly halfway across, and at the far end. Move through those, do not rest in them.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH IS SHARED WITH LIBERTY RIDGE, SO THE ONLY QUESTION THAT MATTERS IS WHERE YOU STOP. Curtis Ridge is the FIRST ridge you meet after crossing the Winthrop. Liberty Ridge is beyond it, past the Carbon.

COUNT THE GLACIERS. Between St Elmo Pass and this base you cross ONE — the Winthrop. If you have dropped onto a SECOND glacier you are on the Carbon and you have walked past Curtis Ridge onto the Liberty Ridge approach.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THE VIEW, AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE ONCE YOU HAVE IT: at about 7,200 ft the ridge gives you snow-free rock ground with the Carbon Glacier and the Willis Wall opening up on the far side. Standing on Curtis Ridge you are looking ACROSS at Willis Wall, not up at it. If the great capped wall is not in front of you, you are not on the ridge yet.

WHAT BEING SHORT LOOKS LIKE, AND IT HAPPENS IN THE DARK: if you walked INTO Glacier Basin and kept going up the valley, you missed the turn for St Elmo Pass. The pass is gained by leaving the basin, not by continuing through it.

WHAT BEING LOW LOOKS LIKE: the traverse holds 7,200 to 7,400 ft deliberately. Losing height on the Winthrop puts you into longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats that run the same way you are walking, which is the worst orientation to fall into one.

ONE MORE THING WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: this ridge is more confusing and more committing than either of its famous neighbours, with 4th-class scrambling through rock bands and at least one rappel on the way UP. If the ground is going smoothly you may be on the wrong feature.
hazards: Serac-threatened sections below the Willis Wall icecap
Loose rock and mixed ground with complex route-finding
Rockfall concentrated at three points on the Winthrop traverse
Longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats running along the line of travel
Remote position with a long exit and no water above St Elmo Pass

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop-to-Carbon traverse under Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.season: Cold, hard-frozen conditions only — a narrow and unpredictable late-spring window, and the route is more often not in condition than in it
approach_variants.notes:
The traditional approach was the Carbon River road to Ipsut Creek and up the Carbon Glacier. Carbon River access has been interrupted for long stretches by bridge and road failure on the state highway that serves it, and when it is out the Carbon side becomes a very long wilderness walk rather than a drive-in. Treat that as a thing to confirm rather than a fixed fact in either direction.

The approach most parties now use starts at White River Campground: Glacier Basin Trail to Glacier Basin, climbers' path to St Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, then rope up, drop onto the Winthrop and traverse west and around beneath Curtis Ridge onto the Carbon Glacier at about 7,300 ft.

From the Carbon, walk up under the wall. Bivy sites exist in the Curtis Ridge access gully and on Curtis Ridge itself.

This is one of the most objectively dangerous pieces of ground in the range. The whole wall is capped by the summit icecap and swept by what comes off it. Nothing in the rack protects you from that; being there in the cold hours does.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS WHAT IS ABOVE YOU, NOT WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU. Willis Wall is capped along its entire top by the hanging summit ice cliff, and all three of its ribs rise from the base of the wall directly above the Carbon Glacier, underneath that cliff. If you are standing beneath a face that is NOT capped by a continuous ice cliff, you are not under Willis Wall.

THE TWO WAYS TO BE WRONG ARE ON OPPOSITE SIDES, AND THE RIDGES NAME THEM. Willis Wall is bounded by CURTIS RIDGE on one side and LIBERTY RIDGE on the other. Facing the wall from the Carbon Glacier, Curtis Ridge is the rib you came around to get here and Liberty Ridge is the rib beyond the far edge of the wall. If you have walked past Liberty Ridge you are under Liberty Wall, which is a different wall with a different reputation.

COUNT THE GLACIERS: TWO. Winthrop, then Carbon. One means you stopped at Curtis Ridge.

THE ROW DOES NOT NAME A RIB, AND THAT IS THE FACT TO CARRY IN. This wall carries three distinct ribs, climbed in different years by different parties and of materially different character. Which one you are under is a decision to be made at the base, from photographs taken before you left, and not something the approach settles for you. Do not treat 'the base of Willis Wall' as though it were one start.

WHAT BEING TOO LATE LOOKS LIKE: nothing visual. The wall does not change. Time of day is the variable that kills here, so the honest base finding is that arriving under it after the sun has been on the icecap means turning round, not looking harder for the rib.
hazards: Extreme objective hazard from the hanging summit icecap seracs, along the entire wall
Continuous rockfall down the face
No easy retreat once committed; a long, serious approach on both sides
Crevassed glacier travel on the Winthrop and Carbon, and again on the summit icecap above
Carbon River road access is intermittently severed, which changes the approach from a drive-in to a multi-day walk

approach_variants.name: Westside Road, Round Pass, St Andrews Park and the Puyallup Cleaver
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun, best frozen; typically out of condition by July
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Westside Road gate near 2,900 ft, about a mile past the Nisqually entrance. The road is gravel and open to vehicles only for the first few miles; beyond that it is foot or bike travel, and has been that way for years because of flood damage in the Tahoma Creek drainage. Treat the walk as part of the route rather than as an inconvenience that might be lifted.

Walk the road roughly 3.5 miles to Round Pass, then take the South Puyallup River Trail to the Wonderland Trail and on to St Andrews Park. Leave the trail there and climb north through alpine meadows onto the Puyallup Cleaver, passing Tokaloo Spire.

Leave the cleaver at about 8,500 ft and traverse the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers into the Sunset Amphitheater. Camps are used on Colonnade Ridge, on the Puyallup Cleaver near 9,000 ft, in the open near 9,600 ft, and at the bergschrund in the amphitheater itself.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION IS A LEAVING, NOT AN ARRIVING, AND IT HAPPENS AT ABOUT 8,500 FT ON THE PUYALLUP CLEAVER. Up to there you are simply walking a ridge. At 8,500 ft you step off it onto glacier and traverse. If you keep climbing the cleaver you will end up over on the Tahoma Glacier side and this route is gone.

PASSING TOKALOO SPIRE IS THE CONFIRMATION THAT YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT CLEAVER. It is the named rock feature on the way up from St Andrews Park. No spire, no cleaver — you left the trail in the wrong place.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS THAT THE GROUND CLOSES AROUND YOU. The Sunset Amphitheater is a bowl shut off by a headwall, with the serac band above it. If you are traversing open glacier that does not close into a bowl, you are still contouring and have not arrived — or you have dropped too low and are heading out across the South Mowich toward the Mowich Face, which is a different climb reached from a different trailhead on the far side of the mountain.

THE CLIMB'S OWN SIGNATURE IS TWO GENDARMES, AND IT CONFIRMS THE ROUTE RATHER THAN THE BASE. Above the steep ground the ridge runs as a knife edge BETWEEN TWO PROMINENT GENDARMES on notably loose, rotten volcanic rock. If the ridge above you has no pair of towers on it, you are on a neighbouring feature.

WHAT THE CRUX LOOKS LIKE, SO YOU KNOW YOU ARE ON IT: roughly 1,000 ft of about 60-degree neve or ice, and it is the only sustained steep ground on the route. Anything shorter and you have not started; anything that keeps going far past that and you are on the amphitheater headwall rather than the ridge.
hazards: Serac and icefall hazard above the Sunset Amphitheater
Rockfall in the amphitheater headwall
A long crevassed traverse of the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers just to reach the base
Rotten volcanic rock on the knife-edge ridge between the gendarmes
Remote west-side position with a road walk at both ends of a very long day

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan Ridge camp, then across the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun for ice; the face bares out and starts shedding rock as it warms
approach_variants.notes:
Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and seasonal. In a normal year it opens well after the roads on the east and south sides of the park — commonly not until July — and closes with the first significant snow. Access to it along the state highway from the north has also been interrupted by bridge failure for extended periods, in which case Mowich Lake itself becomes a long wilderness walk from another park entrance. Confirm which of those two situations applies before you commit a trip to this side.

From Mowich Lake, follow the Wonderland Trail roughly 3-4 miles through Spray Park, passing Spray Falls. Where the Wonderland begins to descend toward the Carbon River, leave it and head cross-country southeast BETWEEN ECHO ROCK AND OBSERVATION ROCK, picking up a climbers' path onto the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge.

Camps sit on the ridge between roughly 9,600 and 10,300 ft, some with old rock wind walls; these serve the Mowich Face, the Edmunds Headwall and Ptarmigan Ridge alike. From camp you DROP and traverse the North Mowich Glacier, roped, watching for fresh rockfall debris on the ice, to gain the base of the face.

There is no water above Spray Park and no maintained trail for the upper two-thirds of this approach.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO NAMED ROCKS ARE THE ONLY HARD MARKERS ON THE WHOLE CROSS-COUNTRY SECTION, AND THEY WORK IN CLOUD BECAUSE THEY ARE BIG AND THEY ARE A PAIR. You leave the Wonderland Trail and go BETWEEN ECHO ROCK AND OBSERVATION ROCK. Not past one of them — between the two. If you can only see one rock, you do not yet know which one it is.

THE SECOND THING IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IT IS WHERE PARTIES GO WRONG: FROM HIGH CAMP YOU GO DOWN. Camp is on Ptarmigan Ridge; the face is across the North Mowich Glacier from it. If you leave camp and start climbing, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge, which is a different route to a different top-out. Losing height off the ridge is correct and is the single clearest signal that you are on this climb and not its neighbour.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE ARRIVAL AND IT IS FREQUENTLY NOT PASSABLE DIRECT. It has to be turned, so budget time for looking rather than treating the schrund as a formality. Reaching a schrund you cannot cross straight over means you are probably in the right place.

THIS IS THE UMBRELLA FACE, NOT A SINGLE LINE, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO CARRY IN. Four separate climbs share this wall and this camp — the North Mowich Headwall, the Central Mowich Face, the Edmunds Headwall, and Ptarmigan Ridge above and to the side of them. They are told apart by WHICH GLACIER you cross from camp and by WHAT THE FIRST GROUND ABOVE THE SCHRUND IS, not by the walk in, which is identical for all of them. Decide which one you are doing before you leave camp in the dark; there is roughly 4,000 ft of 40 to 55 degree ice and mixed ground above, and being one line out is not a thing you discover early.

WHAT RETREAT LOOKS LIKE, BECAUSE IT IS NOT THE WAY YOU CAME: there is no walk-off from the top of this face. Topping out commits you to a carryover down the far side of the mountain to Paradise or White River and a shuttle back. Backing off means reversing the North Mowich Glacier, climbing about 1,000 ft of scree and talus near Observation Rock, and walking out through Spray Park.
hazards: Sustained steep ice and snow with multiple line options and no obvious separation between them
Serac and rockfall hazard on the face; the North Mowich crossing collects the debris
A bergschrund that is frequently impassable direct and must be turned
Roped glacier travel with crevasses under thin snow bridges on both the drop from camp and the return
No walk-off: topping out commits the party to a carryover and a car shuttle
Seasonal road access on this side is late and has been interrupted for long periods

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park to the bivy between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, climbed early in the day for rockfall
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Mowich Face approach and is shared with three other climbs: Mowich Lake, the Wonderland Trail through Spray Park, then cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock onto the climbers' path up lower Ptarmigan Ridge.

The bivouac for this route sits at roughly 9,600 to 10,000 ft on the divide BETWEEN the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers. Two days to reach it is the normal plan rather than a cautious one.

From the bivy the climbing starts almost at once. Above the hourglass, roughly 2,000 ft of about 45-degree snow leads to a rock band; the documented way through is to look for an arch in the rock on the right, traverse left, then work back right to gain the ice cap. In a low-snow year that band can demand unprotected loose 5th-class climbing, which is the part of this route that changes most from season to season.

Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and typically opens around July, and highway access from the north has been severed for extended periods. Confirm before committing.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FOUR CLIMBS SHARE THIS WALL AND THIS CAMP. From the divide bivy the discriminator is WHICH GLACIER YOU CROSS AND WHERE THE HOURGLASS IS.

THE POSITIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE STRONG ONE: THIS ROUTE'S HOURGLASS IS LOW. Within 40 to 50 ft of leaving the bivy you should be in a STEEP CONSTRICTION OF MIXED ROCK AND ICE. First ground, immediately, right off the deck. That is the North Mowich Headwall's signature.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS MOST IS THE CENTRAL MOWICH FACE NEXT DOOR, AND IT ALSO HAS AN HOURGLASS — BUT AT 12,500 FT, NOT AT 10,000. So the question at the base is not 'is there an hourglass on this route' but 'is the hourglass HERE, NOW, in the first 50 ft'. If your first 2,000 ft is open snow with no constriction at all, you are on the Central Mowich Face and your hourglass is still two thousand feet above you.

THE OTHER NEGATIVE IS THE EDMUNDS HEADWALL, AND IT IS SETTLED BY THE SCHRUND: the Edmunds is entered by bypassing its bergschrund on climber's LEFT near a pair of TWIN GENDARMES. If you crossed the schrund beside two rock towers, you are on the Edmunds and you crossed the wrong glacier out of camp.

SEQUENCE CHECK ONCE COMMITTED, IN ORDER: 40-50 ft hourglass of rock and ice, then roughly 2,000 ft of sustained 45-degree snow, then a rock band that has to be cleared. If the rock band arrives early, you are not on this line. If it never arrives, you traversed off onto the Central Mowich, which skirts the band entirely by going right.

WHAT BEING TOO FAR ROUND LOOKS LIKE: if you left camp and CLIMBED rather than crossing a glacier, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge.
hazards: A rock band crux that can require unprotected loose 5th-class climbing in low-snow years
Sustained steep ice with rockfall exposure — climb it early
Crevasses and avalanche debris on the glacier crossing out of camp
Remote position, two-day approach, and no quick retreat from high on the face
Seasonal and intermittently severed road access on this side of the park

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and lower Ptarmigan Ridge, then 1,000 ft down to the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug
approach_variants.notes:
Wonderland Trail from Mowich Lake about 4 miles to Spray Park, then the climbers' path up lower Ptarmigan Ridge. At about 8,300 ft the route DESCENDS roughly 1,000 ft onto the North Mowich Glacier and crosses to the base of the face.

There are two lines from about 12,500 ft. The original variation cuts LEFT into an hourglass of snow, ice and rock, gaining a ledge that leads to a 40-50 degree ramp to the top. The harder variation cuts RIGHT through a couple of AI2-3 ice steps and four to six pitches of 50-60 degree snow to the same high point.

Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and typically opens around July; highway access to it from the north has been severed for long periods. Confirm current access before planning around this trailhead.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST THING TO GET RIGHT IS THAT YOU LOSE A THOUSAND FEET ON THE WAY IN. At about 8,300 ft on lower Ptarmigan Ridge you stop climbing and drop onto the North Mowich Glacier. A party that keeps gaining height is on Ptarmigan Ridge, not on this face, and will not find out for hours.

FOUR CLIMBS COME OFF THIS WALL AND THEY ARE SEPARATED BY WHERE THE STEEP GROUND IS, NOT BY THE WALK IN.

THE POSITIVE TEST FOR THIS ROUTE IS AN ABSENCE, WHICH IS UNUSUAL BUT IT IS THE RELIABLE ONE HERE: THERE IS NO CONSTRICTION LOW DOWN. You cross the schrund and climb open face. The hourglass on this route is HIGH — around 12,500 ft — not at the bottom. So if your first 50 ft above the schrund is a steep pinch of mixed rock and ice, you are on the North Mowich Headwall and you crossed too far round.

THE ROCK BAND SETTLES IT DEFINITIVELY, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE THE TWO LINES BEHAVE OPPOSITELY. On this face, at the rock band you can TRAVERSE RIGHT SEVERAL HUNDRED FEET AND SKIRT THE BAND ENTIRELY. On the North Mowich Headwall you cannot: you have to clear the band, at 5th class in a lean year. If the band in front of you has to be climbed rather than walked around, you are one line over.

SCHRUND CHECK: the bergschrund under the central face has been passed by a bypass through a rock band on climber's LEFT. If the only way across in front of you is beside a pair of twin gendarmes, that is the Edmunds Headwall's schrund and you are further round the mountain than you meant to be.

CHOOSE YOUR VARIATION BEFORE 12,500 FT, NOT AT IT. Left is the original: an hourglass, a ledge, a 40-50 degree ramp. Right is harder: AI2-3 ice steps and four to six pitches of 50-60 degree snow. They rejoin, but you cannot swap once you are on one.
hazards: Ice steps and steep snow with rockfall exposure
A 1,000 ft descent onto the glacier on the approach, which must be reclimbed if you retreat
Remote approach with limited bailout options
Crevasses on the North Mowich crossing
Seasonal and intermittently severed road access on this side of the park

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park to the 9,600 ft divide, then across to the Edmunds Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul; the headwall turns icier and starts shedding rock as summer goes on
approach_variants.notes:
Shared Mowich Face approach: Mowich Lake, the Wonderland Trail through Spray Park, then cross-country onto lower Ptarmigan Ridge and up to the bivouac at roughly 9,600 ft on the divide between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers. Rangers and climbing parties have both used that divide bivy as the base for this route.

From there, cross the glacier to the foot of the headwall. Parties commonly leave the bivy around 2 am and reach the base a few hours later; the crossing runs beneath the ice cliff run-out coming off the upper mountain, so it is a place to move rather than a place to sort gear.

The headwall itself is sustained steep snow and ice from roughly 9,900 to 13,400 ft, and its character swings between firm penitente neve and a considerably icier chute depending on the year. Above it the route traverses toward Liberty Cap on ground that can be heavily penitente-covered and slow.

Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and typically opens around July; highway access from the north has been interrupted for extended periods.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FOUR CLIMBS LEAVE THE SAME DIVIDE BIVY. THE SCHRUND IS WHAT TELLS THEM APART FOR THIS ONE.

THE POSITIVE TEST, AND IT IS A PAIR OF OBJECTS RATHER THAN A DESCRIPTION, WHICH IS WHY IT WORKS IN POOR LIGHT: the bergschrund bypass for the Edmunds Headwall is on CLIMBER'S LEFT, NEAR TWIN GENDARMES. Two rock towers, and you go left of the schrund beside them. No twin gendarmes means no Edmunds Headwall.

THE NEGATIVE AGAINST THE NEIGHBOUR ON ONE SIDE: the North Mowich Headwall opens with a 40 to 50 ft HOURGLASS of steep rock and ice within a rope length of the bivy. If your first ground is a tight mixed pinch rather than a schrund crossing beside gendarmes, you crossed the wrong glacier.

THE NEGATIVE AGAINST THE NEIGHBOUR ON THE OTHER SIDE: the Central Mowich Face's schrund is turned by a rock-band bypass on climber's left with no gendarmes at it, and its steep ground eases before 13,000 ft. This route is sustained a long way further — about 9,900 to 13,400 ft is the whole headwall.

THE CONDITION TEST TELLS YOU WHICH DAY YOU HAVE, AND IT IS WORTH MAKING AT THE SCHRUND RATHER THAN AT 12,000 FT: firm penitentes mean kicking and slow but secure progress; a bare icy chute means screws, and the same face is a different climb. Decide before you commit — there is no easy way off the middle of it.

THE TOP-OUT IS NOT THE MOUNTAIN'S SUMMIT. This route finishes at or below LIBERTY CAP, on the northwest rim, not at Columbia Crest. Standing on Liberty Cap and looking across at higher ground is correct, not a navigational error.
hazards: Sustained steep snow and ice from about 9,900 to 13,400 ft
Rockfall and icefall down the headwall once it warms
Crevasses on the Edmunds and South Mowich approach
A glacier crossing beneath the upper-mountain ice cliff run-out
Penitente ground above the headwall that can make the exit far slower than the climb
Remote, committing position with no walk-off from the top of the face

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson Glacier to the narrow couloir
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun; a south-facing snow line that wants a hard overnight freeze and an early start
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise, drop southwest onto the Nisqually Moraine and onto the Nisqually Glacier, cross it westward, then work up the Wilson Gully, the Wilson Bench and the Wilson Chute on the west side of the glacier toward the camps near The Castle around 9,000-9,500 ft.

From camp, continue northwest to the foot of the couloir. Summit day from that camp is commonly 5 to 7 hours.

The couloir is about 50-degree snow and ice. It merges with the Fuhrer Finger on the west side of the Nisqually at roughly 11,500 ft, so above that point the two routes are one.

Most parties descend the Fuhrer Finger or the upper Kautz and the standard route back to Camp Muir and Paradise rather than reversing this line. There is no water above Paradise.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAND ON THE UPPER WILSON GLACIER AND LOOK UP. FROM LEFT TO RIGHT THE THREE FEATURES ARE: THE WILSON GLACIER HEADWALL, THE FUHRER THUMB, THE FUHRER FINGER. Learn that order before you leave the car — it is the only thing separating this route from its two neighbours in the dark, and all three start within a short distance of each other off the same bench of glacier.

THE THUMB IS THE MIDDLE ONE AND IT IS THE NARROW ONE. That is the whole test, and it is a shape test, which is what you want when you cannot see the mountain.

THE POSITIVE-NEGATIVE PAIR THAT SETTLES IT: THE FINGER IS WIDE AND FUNNELS THROUGH AN OBVIOUS HOURGLASS at around 10,000 ft on the eastern side of the headwall. THE THUMB IS THE NARROWER COULOIR IMMEDIATELY WEST OF IT. So if the gully in front of you is broad and necks down through a conspicuous hourglass, you are at the Finger and the Thumb is one gully to your LEFT as you face uphill. If you are looking at an open face rather than into a gully at all, you have gone one too far left and you are under the Wilson Glacier Headwall, which is a harder proposition than either couloir.

CONFIRMATION ON THE CLIMB: the two couloirs MERGE at about 11,500 ft on the west side of the Nisqually. So being one gully out becomes invisible above that height, which cuts both ways — it means a mistake is survivable, and it means you cannot use the upper mountain to work out which one you climbed. Settle it at the bottom.

WHAT BEING TOO EARLY IN THE APPROACH LOOKS LIKE: if you have not crossed the Nisqually Glacier westward, you have not started. Everything about this route is on the west side of that glacier, under The Castle and the Kautz Ice Cliff.
hazards: Rockfall funnelling through a steep, narrow couloir with no shelter in it
Icefall off the Kautz Ice Cliff onto the approach traverse
Wet-snow avalanche on this south aspect once it warms — an early start is the protection
Crevasses on the Nisqually and Wilson glaciers
The Finger and the Thumb merge high, so a misidentification cannot be detected above 11,500 ft

approach_variants.name: Westside Road and Tahoma Creek to St Andrews Rock, then the Sickle
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, best in June; a west aspect that holds firmer snow later into the morning than the south-side routes
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Westside Road gate at the Dry Creek trailhead near 2,900 ft. The road is gated to vehicles a few miles in because of repeated Tahoma Creek flooding and debris flows; the remainder is walked or biked, and has been for years. Plan the road as part of the climb.

From the gate, take the Tahoma Creek Trail up to the Wonderland Trail near 5,600 ft, then onto the southern side of the Tahoma Glacier. Camps are used near Emerald Ridge lower down and around 9,800-10,400 ft near St Andrews Rock.

The glacier is climbed with a series of diagonal traverses: zigzag the south side to about 7,200 ft, then traverse back and forth around 9,000-10,000 ft to get through crevasse bands, then into the Sickle and out onto the plateau near 12,600 ft.

Car-to-car this is a very long outing — a documented itinerary from the road closure ran about 21.5 miles.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ST ANDREWS ROCK IS THE RECOGNITION POINT, AND THE THING THAT CONFIRMS IT IS THAT YOU GO DOWN.

You climb to a ridge just short of 10,000 ft BELOW ST ANDREWS ROCK, and then you DROP several hundred feet on a ramp onto the Tahoma Glacier proper at around 9,600 ft. Losing that height is correct. It is the clearest single signal that you are on this route: a party that never gives height back has stayed on the Puyallup Cleaver and is heading for Sunset Ridge, one drainage north.

THE SICKLE IS THE SECOND MARKER AND IT IS A SHAPE, NOT A PLACE. At about 11,200 ft the route enters a NARROW CHUTE THAT CURVES LEFT AROUND A CLIFF — the reason it is called the Sickle. If you are climbing straight up open glacier with no constriction and no cliff to curve around, you are still below it, whatever the altimeter says.

CLIMB THE SICKLE ON ITS NORTH SIDE, KEEPING LEFT OF THE ICY RIDGES, to the plateau at about 12,600 ft. Topping the Sickle is the point at which you are out of the icefall run-out, and that is the honest marker for 'the dangerous part is behind you'.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS FOR TIMING RATHER THAN NAVIGATION: the traverse below the Sickle runs under its run-out zone, which funnels ice debris. There is no line through that avoids it. Being there in the dark and frozen is the only protection, so if you arrive at the base of the Sickle in the sun, the finding is that you should not be there, not that you should look for a better line.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG SIDE LOOKS LIKE LOW DOWN: the route works the SOUTHERN side of the glacier from the Wonderland Trail at 5,600 ft. Drifting north early puts you into the crevasse bands the diagonal traverses exist to avoid.
hazards: Complex crevasse navigation with several bands that have to be traversed around
Serac and icefall hazard in and below the Sickle, with unavoidable run-out exposure on the traverse
A long road walk at both ends and a very long car-to-car day
Route-finding on a committing west-side approach with no maintained trail above 5,600 ft
Thin late-season snow bridges over the upper glacier

approach_variants.name: Paradise and the Muir route partway, then west to the Turtle and Camp Hazard
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-May to early Aug; the ice holds into summer but the approach and glacier conditions degrade quickly after the start of August
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise at 5,400 ft, the common approach follows the Camp Muir route via the Skyline Trail and the Muir Snowfield partway, then cuts west. The route crosses the lower Nisqually, gains the Wilson Glacier and climbs to the Turtle Snowfield, with camps at The Castle around 9,200-9,500 ft and Camp Hazard at 10,800 ft at the top of the snowfield.

Roped travel and crevasse-rescue readiness are needed from the moment you leave the Nisqually. Water is available from snowmelt lower down on the Comet Falls and Van Trump side but not once you are on glacier ice.

Rockfall and icefall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall are the approach-zone hazards; move through the exposed ground early and efficiently.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HEADWALL AND THE STANDARD KAUTZ CHUTE ARE TWO DIFFERENT LINES OFF THE SAME CAMP, AND THE TEST IS HOW MANY STEEP STEPS YOU MEET.

COUNT TWO. This route presents as TWO ICE STEPS SEPARATED BY A BAND OF LOWER-ANGLE SNOW: the lower step around 50 degrees, the upper around 70. Step, bench, step. If you climb one sustained runnel and the angle then eases the whole way to the summit plateau, you were in the standard Kautz ice chute, not on the headwall.

THE UPPER STEP IS THE ONE THAT SETTLES IT — noticeably steeper and more sustained than the lower, needing two tools and screws in ice that is often harder or more brittle. The lower step is broad and stepped out and rarely steeper than about 35-40 degrees, and most parties get up it with a single tool and a couple of screws. If the harder ground came FIRST, you are not on this.

WHERE YOU ROPE UP IS PART OF THE FINDING: on the Turtle or Wilson Glacier BELOW the headwall, often after a short rappel or a fixed-line downclimb off the bivy rock at Camp Hazard. Descending off camp before you climb is correct and is a good sign you are on the right line rather than walking out along the chute.

THE APPROACH HAS TWO STARTS AND THEY LAND IN THE SAME PLACE, SO DO NOT LET THE DIFFERENCE UNSETTLE YOU: Paradise and the Muir route cutting west, or the Comet Falls and Van Trump Park trail from a lower trailhead. Both cross the Nisqually onto the Wilson and climb the Turtle. If you find yourself on maintained trail beside a waterfall you are on the second of those, not lost.

WHAT BEING TOO LATE LOOKS LIKE: seracs and rockfall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall hang over the steep ground. The upper step must be climbed efficiently and early. The honest reading of arriving at it warm and in the sun is to go down.
hazards: Two steep ice steps beneath serac and rockfall from the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall
Brittle or hard ice on the upper step, with screws the only protection
Genuinely complex crevassed glacier travel on the Kautz approach
A short rappel or fixed-line downclimb off the Camp Hazard bivy rock to reach the base
Descent rappels are on ice anchors you build yourself; old ascent-placed threads must not be reused

approach_variants.name: Silver Falls loop from the Ohanapecosh side
approach_variants.season: Roughly late spring through fall, whenever the southeast corner of the park is open to vehicles
approach_variants.notes:
This is a single roadside boulder at about 1,900 ft in old forest, not an alpine objective, and the approach is a walk on maintained trail with essentially no gain.

From the Ohanapecosh day-use area, follow the Silver Falls Loop about a mile. The loop can also be picked up from the Grove of the Patriarchs end via the Eastside Trail, which is the alternative when work on the campground side has closed the near entrance — that corridor has been under reconstruction in recent seasons, so check which end of the loop is open rather than assuming either.

The road serving this corner of the park is seasonal: normally open from late spring through fall and gated in winter.

No climbing permit is involved. The park's climbing permit and its blue-bag rules apply to parties travelling on glaciers or above 10,000 ft, which this is not; the park entrance fee still applies.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS THAT YOU NEVER LEAVE THE TRAIL. The boulder sits a few feet off the Silver Falls Loop, roughly a mile round from the Ohanapecosh day-use area. If you have stepped off maintained tread, started bushwhacking, or gained more than about a hundred feet, you have walked past it — go back rather than searching uphill.

THE SHAPE IS THE NAME: a low boulder with a loaf-shaped top hold, climbed on its left side. One problem, a couple of moves.

THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE IS ABOUT THE WHOLE OUTING RATHER THAN THE LAST HUNDRED YARDS, AND IT IS WORTH STATING BECAUSE THIS ROUTE IS FILED UNDER THE MOUNTAIN: if you are on snow, on a glacier, or anywhere above a few thousand feet, you are not near this boulder and never will be. It is in low forest in the southeast corner of the park, tens of miles and twelve thousand feet from the summit routes filed beside it.

WATER AND ESCAPE ARE NON-PROBLEMS HERE — the loop has running water nearby and you can walk out either way round it. That is the honest description; do not carry mountain planning onto it.
hazards: Nothing alpine — the real risks are trail closures and construction in this corner of the park
Landing on forest floor with roots and uneven ground
Seasonal road closure to the southeast entrance in winter

approach_variants.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHITMAN NOTCH AT ABOUT 9,100 FT IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU KNOW IT BY WHAT BECOMES VISIBLE RATHER THAN BY THE ALTIMETER: IT IS THE FIRST PLACE THE WHITMAN GLACIER COMES INTO VIEW. Until you can see a SECOND glacier on the far side, you have not reached the notch.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING PROPER IS HIGHER STILL, AND IT IS A CHANGE OF SURFACE: at about 10,500-11,000 ft the snow ends and a loose rock-and-scree gully begins. That transition is the base. The sequence above it is countable and in this order: gully, a SHORT step of about 6 ft, a gully-chimney, the summit notch, then an exposed scramble along the crest.

THE ROUTE-FINDING TRAP IS LOW, NOT HIGH, AND IT IS THE ONE THING ON THIS CLIMB THAT REGULARLY COMMITS PARTIES TO BAD GROUND: between Summerland and Meany Crest, IF YOU FIND YOURSELF CONTOURING CLIMBER'S RIGHT INTO A BOWL UNDER ROCK BANDS, YOU ARE CLIFFED OUT AND OFF THE LINE. The cairned and boot-packed line stays left of that bowl. Fix this by going back to the last cairn, not by traversing further.

THE SUMMIT-CREST TEST IS A NEGATIVE AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS: the last 30 to 100 ft is a narrow crumbling andesite crest with roughly 2,000 ft dropping away to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. If the ground is not falling away on both sides of you, you have not reached the true summit — you are on the notch or a subsidiary block below it.

TIMING AS A FINDING: the andesite loosens as the sun works on it, and the crevasse bridges soften through the day. Being at the notch early is not tidiness, it is the whole plan.
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
A bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, with about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side

approach_variants.name: Paradise and the Muir route to 8,600 ft, then east through the Cathedral Rocks notch
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-May. This is the winter and early-spring line, used precisely when the White River road to Summerland is shut and the Fryingpan approach is unavailable
approach_variants.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route exits the upper Frying Pan Glacier's corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION IS AT 8,600 FT AND IT IS A LEAVING, NOT AN ARRIVING. You step off the Camp Muir track while still about 1,500 ft BELOW Camp Muir. IF YOU REACH CAMP MUIR YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR — by a vertical quarter of a mile, on the busiest bootpack on the mountain, which is exactly why it happens.

COUNT WHAT YOU CROSS: THREE GLACIERS AND ONE ROCK CLEAVER, in this order — Paradise, Cowlitz, then a NOTCH IN CATHEDRAL ROCKS, then the Ingraham. If you have crossed the Cowlitz and walked into rock without finding a notch, you are BELOW the notch and need to regain height. The traverse deliberately holds elevation to stay above a serac and cliff band; drifting down is the error that feels easy at the time.

THE BASE IS A RAMP, AND IT IS THE ONLY ramp: a snow or rock ramp at about 8,900 ft leading onto the south and east face. Arriving at the foot of a face with no ramp means you are round the wrong side of it.

THE NEGATIVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM THE PEAK'S OTHER ROUTE: the standard line on Little Tahoma comes from the FRYINGPAN side, over Whitman Notch, from the east. This one comes from PARADISE, from the southwest, and never goes near Summerland or Meany Crest. If you are looking for a notch between two glaciers with the Whitman below you, you are on the other route.

WHY THIS ROUTE EXISTS AND WHEN IT STOPS WORKING: it is the winter line, done before the Cowlitz and Ingraham become too broken to cross safely. Once those glaciers open up, the traverse is the hazard rather than the climb.
hazards: Serac fall and crevasse hazard across an extended Cowlitz and Ingraham traverse
A cliff and serac band immediately below the traverse line, which is why elevation must be held
Wind-slab avalanche potential on the ramp gaining the face in early season
Loose rock in the summit gully-chimney and on the final crest scramble
A long committing traverse with the same ground to reverse on the way out

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek, the PCT and High Camp, then across the lava fields to the Lava Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun. This is a cold-season face: it turns icy and starts shedding rock as the snowpack recedes later in summer
approach_variants.notes:
From the Killen Creek trailhead on the forest road near Takhlakh Lake at about 4,140 ft, follow Killen Creek Trail #113 roughly 3.1 miles through open lodgepole forest, crossing East Fork Adams Creek near mile 2.5, to the PCT at about 6,100 ft. Cross the PCT onto the High Camp Trail #10 for another mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, about 6,900 ft, on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine.

From High Camp this route is reached more directly than the Lyman: traverse off-trail east across the lava fields to the toe of the Lava Glacier, without needing to work around Lava Ridge.

The approach roads are gravel and seasonal, opening as snow clears.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE RIDGES. THAT IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM ON THIS SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, AND IT IS COUNTABLE IN CLOUD.

From High Camp the features run in this order as you work east: the ADAMS GLACIER, then the NORTH RIDGE (the North Cleaver), then the LAVA GLACIER, then LAVA RIDGE, then the LYMAN GLACIER. Three glaciers, two ridges between them, in that order.

THIS ROUTE'S BASE IS AT THE HEAD OF THE LAVA GLACIER — SO YOU CROSS ONE RIDGE PAST THE NORTH RIDGE AND STOP. IF YOU HAVE ROUNDED OR CROSSED A SECOND RIDGE, YOU ARE AT THE LYMAN GLACIER AND ON A DIFFERENT CLIMB.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A SHAPE, AND IT IS THE reason this route is worth doing: THE HEADWALL IS A TRIANGLE. It is the face closing between the North Ridge on one side and Lava Ridge on the other, the two of them converging above you. If the ground ahead is open glacier that does not narrow to a point, you are not under the headwall — you are on the glacier below it, and the apron will keep going for a while yet.

THE NEGATIVE THAT CATCHES PEOPLE IS THE NORTH RIDGE ITSELF, because it is the walk-off and it is right there: if you are climbing snow with a rocky cleaver on one hand and no closing headwall above, you are on the North Ridge, which is the descent for this route rather than the ascent.

CONFIRMATION ONCE COMMITTED: about 45-degree neve, climbed nearly continuously without belays because stopping under it is worse than moving. The first ascent went from 8,500 ft to the summit in around five and a half hours. If you are placing gear on every rope length you are not moving the way this face wants to be moved.

TIMING AS A FINDING: this face is graded for cold. Arriving at the triangle with the sun on it means going down, not looking for a better line.
hazards: Steep ice and snow with serac hazard on a face that must be climbed continuously
Rockfall increasing sharply as the headwall warms
Crevasse navigation on the Lava Glacier apron
A long descent of the North Ridge on loose volcanic scree with rockfall onto parties below
Seasonal gravel road access that opens late in a heavy year

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek and High Camp, then east past Lava Ridge to the Lyman at 8,000 ft
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul; climbed in late spring and early summer as moderate to steep snow and sometimes alpine ice
approach_variants.notes:
From the Killen Creek trailhead, follow Trail #113 through open dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows — the last easy water before the high basin. The trees thin as the trail climbs rockier ground to the PCT at about 6,100 ft, roughly 3.1 miles in. Continue straight across onto High Camp Trail #10 for about a mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, near 6,900 ft.

From High Camp the maintained trail is done. Traverse east and southeast off-trail across lava fields, across the toe of the Lava Glacier and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, to the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This is glacier and talus travel with real route-finding, worst in a low-snow year; rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on ice.

Most of the route can be simul-climbed with a running belay on pickets. The standard descent is the North Ridge, not a reversal — long, loose volcanic scree, occasionally narrow, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE RIDGES, AND FOR THIS ROUTE YOU MUST GET PAST TWO.

East of High Camp the order is: ADAMS GLACIER, NORTH RIDGE, LAVA GLACIER, LAVA RIDGE, LYMAN GLACIER. You cross the Lava Glacier and then go around or over the TOE OF LAVA RIDGE. Lava Ridge is the second ridge and it is the gate. If you have crossed only one ridge and stopped at a glacier, you are at the Lava Glacier Headwall — a different climb with a triangular face — not at the Lyman.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A FORK, AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE ONCE YOU ARE ON IT: THE LYMAN SPLITS AROUND A NARROW ROCK OUTCROP into two lobes. The north lobe is the original line; the south lobe runs 40-degree unbroken neve on its lower half and is broken by crevasses and serac walls on its upper half. A glacier that forks around an island of rock is the confirmation you are where you meant to be.

THE CRUX CONFIRMS IT A SECOND TIME, HIGHER: both lobes lead to a chute near 10,000 ft that runs anywhere from 45 to 65 degrees over about 50 ft depending on the year. One short steep chute, then easier snow to the summit plateau. If you meet no constriction at all, you are on a neighbouring glacier.

THE BASE ELEVATION IS THE THIRD CHECK: about 8,000 ft. Arriving on ice much higher than that means you gained the glacier well above its toe and may have come onto it over the ridge rather than around it, which is fine but changes where the lobes sit relative to you.

WHAT THE DESCENT MEANS FOR THE APPROACH, AND IT IS WORTH DECIDING AT THE CAR: you do not come back this way. The walk-off is the North Ridge, back toward High Camp. So the ridge you counted past on the way in is not the ridge you come down.
hazards: Crevasse and serac navigation on the Lyman, particularly on the south lobe's upper half
A short steep crux chute near 10,000 ft that varies from 45 to 65 degrees year to year
Long sustained high-altitude climbing with a late-season low-snow route-finding problem on the traverse
A descent down the North Ridge on loose rotten volcanic scree, with rockfall onto parties below
Seasonal gravel road access

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain Trail east around the mountain
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun for the headwall itself; the surrounding east-side walls are rockfall-prone once warm
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cold Springs and South Climb trailhead at about 5,600 ft at the end of the forest road north of Trout Lake, follow South Climb Trail #183 about a mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail.

Instead of continuing north toward the Lunch Counter, follow the Round the Mountain Trail east and then north, contouring below the Crescent Glacier and around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Wilson and Klickitat glacier basins. This is a long, mostly off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands.

The Wilson descends from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft, and it is split by a rock rib. Expect a full day to reach a camp near its toe before any summit attempt.

This is one of the least-visited and least-documented flanks of the mountain. The descent is not a reversal: parties top out and come down the standard South Climb to Cold Springs.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION HAPPENS ABOUT A MILE FROM THE CAR AND IT IS A TURNING, NOT AN ARRIVAL. At the junction of the South Climb Trail with the Round the Mountain Trail, the standard South Spur route goes NORTH toward the Lunch Counter; this route goes EAST. If you are climbing toward the Lunch Counter, you are on the standard South Climb and this route is already behind you.

THAT IS THE ONE ERROR WORTH GUARDING, BECAUSE IT IS RECOVERABLE ONLY BY WALKING BACK DOWN. Everything after it is a long contour.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS A GLACIER SPLIT BY A ROCK RIB. The Wilson runs from about 10,600 ft down to about 7,400 ft and a rock rib divides it. A headwall above a glacier that is bisected by a rib is the confirmation. An unbroken glacier with no rib in it is not the Wilson.

THE SECOND POSITIVE IS ASPECT AND IT IS THE COARSEST BUT MOST RELIABLE: you must be on the EAST side of the mountain. Going around the eastern flank is the whole approach. If the sun is rising behind the mountain rather than in front of you, you have not come far enough round.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS FOR SAFETY RATHER THAN NAVIGATION: the contour runs directly beneath cliff bands that shed rock. It is a place to keep moving. Persistent rockfall on these east-side headwalls is among the reasons most of them remain unrepeated, so a rope-length of comfortable ground is not evidence the ground above you is quiet.

WHAT BEING ON A NEIGHBOURING BASIN LOOKS LIKE: keep going round and you reach the Klickitat basin. The Wilson is the first of the two you meet coming from the south.
hazards: Persistent rockfall from the east-side cliff bands, directly over the contouring approach
A steep ice and snow headwall with serac hazard
Crevasse navigation on the Wilson
A long, mostly off-trail traverse with creek crossings and route-finding, and a full day just to reach camp
Rarely climbed, so conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic and rescue would be slow

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek and High Camp, then the north-facing slope below the Adams Glacier terminus
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul, on neve
approach_variants.notes:
Forest roads from the Takhlakh Lake area to the Killen Creek trailhead, then Killen Creek Trail #113 to the PCT junction and High Camp Trail #10 to the meadow camp at about 6,900 ft.

From camp, gain the north-facing slope that sits between the Adams Glacier and the crest of the Northwest Ridge. The line deliberately gains access BELOW the Adams Glacier terminus to avoid its crevasses and moats, then follows steepening 40 to 45 degree neve past a narrow rock-band pinch to the ridge crest near 10,000 ft and on to the summit.

The ridge crest itself is avoided on purpose: the rock on it is poor.

Descent is along the North Ridge back to the Adams Glacier basin high camp, or in ski conditions the route itself can be reversed, threading the same rock-band pinch.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS THE GROUND BETWEEN TWO THINGS, SO THE TEST IS THAT YOU HAVE ONE ON EACH SIDE.

AS YOU CLIMB, THE ADAMS GLACIER SHOULD BE ON YOUR RIGHT AND THE CREST OF THE NORTHWEST RIDGE ON YOUR LEFT. If both are on the same side of you, you are on one of them rather than between them, and you are not on this route.

THE ROCK IS THE NEGATIVE ON ONE SIDE, AND IT IS TACTILE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WANT AT NIGHT: this line stays OFF the crest because the crest's rock is poor. If you are pulling on loose blocky rock instead of kicking steps in neve, you have drifted left onto the ridge.

THE CREVASSES ARE THE NEGATIVE ON THE OTHER SIDE: the route gains its ground BELOW the Adams Glacier terminus specifically so it does not have to deal with the glacier's crevasses and moats. If you are stepping across crevasses, you are too far right and on the Adams Glacier route, which is a different and harder climb.

THE POSITIVE, AND IT IS COUNTABLE: ONE CONSTRICTION. A narrow pinch through a rock band, ski-width or body-width, is the crux and the only place the route squeezes. If you have climbed a couple of thousand feet of 40 to 45 degree neve and met no constriction, the pinch is still above you and you are on route. If you met a constriction in the first rope length, you are somewhere else.

WHAT THE PINCH MEANS FOR CONDITIONS: it gets tighter in a low-snow year, which is when it becomes the AI2-3 crux rather than a step. It is also a terrain trap — you are between cliff bands there with limited escape, so decide about it from below rather than at it.

TOP-OUT CHECK: the route joins the NORTHWEST RIDGE CREST near 10,000 ft. Gaining a crest at that height is correct; gaining one much lower means you climbed onto the ridge early instead of past it.
hazards: A terrain trap between cliff bands with limited escape once committed mid-route
A narrow rock-band pinch that tightens to AI2-3 in low-snow years
Crevasse and moat hazard where the route gains ground below the Adams Glacier terminus
Poor rock on the adjacent ridge crest, which is why the line avoids it
Sustained 40-45 degree neve with a running belay the only practical protection

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs, then west around onto the southwest flank
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jul; crevasse hazard grows through the season as the glaciers open up
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cold Springs trailhead, work around onto the mountain's southwest flank using the Round the Mountain trail system, and approach the glacier from below.

The climb is a gently sloping glacier ascent of the Avalanche and White Salmon glaciers, mostly moderate to steep snow to about 40 degrees, simul-climbable, with occasional ice work where the White Salmon has broken up. A steeper headwall variation exists where the two glaciers merge and can be alpine ice late in the season.

Descent is south via the South Spur snowfields, or the snowfield beside the Avalanche and White Salmon glaciers, back toward the Morrison Creek and Cold Springs approach, glissading where conditions allow — so this is a loop off one trailhead rather than an out-and-back.

Forest roads to Cold Springs and Morrison Creek are gravel and open as snow clears.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE SOUTH SPUR YOU ARE ON, AND IT IS A DECISION MADE LOW.

From Cold Springs the standard South Climb goes up the SOUTH SPUR to the Lunch Counter at about 9,300 ft. This route leaves that line and works WEST, round onto the southwest flank, to the Avalanche and White Salmon glaciers. IF THE LUNCH COUNTER IS STILL AHEAD OF YOU OR ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE NOT LEFT THE STANDARD ROUTE.

THE NEGATIVE HERE INVERTS THE USUAL INSTINCT AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL SINGLE MARKER: YOU SHOULD MEET ALMOST NOBODY. The South Spur is the most-travelled route on this mountain and carries a trench and camps most of the season. This flank sees a fraction of that traffic. A boot pack underfoot is evidence you are still on the South Climb, not evidence you are on route.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A JUNCTION OF TWO GLACIERS: the Avalanche and the White Salmon MERGE, and the headwall at that merge is the steeper variation. A single unbroken snow slope with no second glacier joining it is not the base — keep contouring.

THE CONDITION TEST DECIDES WHICH CLIMB YOU GET: the merge headwall is snow early and can break out into alpine ice late, which is why a spare tool and a couple of screws are worth carrying even though most of the route is a walk. If it is bare ice and you brought one axe, that is a finding about the day, not about the route.

WHAT COMING BACK LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS WHY THIS DOES NOT NEED A SHUTTLE: you descend SOUTH off the summit onto the South Spur snowfields and back toward the same trailhead. Reversing the ascent line is not the plan.
hazards: Crevasse hazard that increases through the season as the glacier opens up
Alpine ice at the merge headwall late in the season, on a route otherwise climbed with one axe
Genuine glacier travel on a flank that sees very little traffic, so no track and no other parties
A long contour off the standard route with route-finding on the way round
Seasonal gravel road access

approach_variants.name: Climbers Bivouac and the Ptarmigan Trail to the marked ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Oct for the summer route; full winter conditions with ice axe and crampons can apply well into late spring
approach_variants.notes:
From the Climbers Bivouac trailhead at about 3,700 ft — the highest vehicle access on this side of the mountain — start on the signed Ptarmigan Trail #216A through open forest. It climbs a moderate 1,100 ft over about 2.25 miles to timberline near 4,800 ft. That is the last shade and the last practical water; a couple of small seasonal creeklets cross the lower trail and nothing is reliable above, so most parties carry everything from the car.

At timberline the trail ends and the route moves onto the open volcanic slopes of Monitor Ridge itself: a broad rib of old lava flows flanked by loose pumice and ash.

A permit is required above 4,800 ft year-round and is checked at or near the trailhead.

There is no technical climbing here. It is a long, steep hike and scramble, and the difficulty is navigation and footing rather than terrain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE POSTS ARE THE ROUTE, AND KNOWING WHERE THEY END IS THE WHOLE FINDING.

FROM TIMBERLINE AT ABOUT 4,800 FT TO ABOUT 7,000 FT THE LINE IS MARKED BY LARGE WOODEN POSTS. They end at the monitoring equipment near 7,000 ft. Above that, the last roughly 1,300 ft to the crater rim is unmarked ash, pumice and scattered rock.

SO THE TEST IN FOG IS A NEGATIVE AND IT IS EXACT: IF THE POSTS HAVE STOPPED AND YOU HAVE NOT PASSED THE MONITORING EQUIPMENT, YOU HAVE DRIFTED OFF THE LINE — you have not finished the marked section. Stop and go back to the last post you saw rather than continuing on a bearing. Losing the posts is the single biggest route-finding hazard on this climb, and a small drift puts you on steep loose off-route ground.

THE SURFACE TEST TELLS YOU WHETHER YOU ARE ON THE RIB OR BESIDE IT: the route climbs the ROCK RIBS of old lava. If you are sliding two steps back for every step up in loose ash, you are in the gullies beside the rib. Move onto the rock — it is both faster and a signal you have found the line again.

THE TOP IS NOT WHERE YOU THINK: the crater rim at about 8,363 ft is the top of the climbing, and the true high point is a walk along the rim from where you arrive. Do not treat first sight of the crater as the summit.

AND THE RIM ITSELF IS A NEGATIVE, NOT A MARKER: it is corniced and unstable with a history of fall-throughs. Do not walk to the edge to work out where you are.
hazards: Losing the wooden posts in fog or whiteout, which puts parties onto steep loose off-route ground
Unstable cornices and fall-through risk at the crater rim
Deep loose pumice and ash above 7,000 ft with poor footing in both directions
No water above the lower trail
Full winter conditions and avalanche terrain on the upper slopes well into late spring

approach_variants.name: Marble Mountain Sno-Park and the Swift Creek Trail to Worm Flow Ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, with the best conditions typically Feb-Apr when the snowpack is deep enough to bury the loose ash and consolidated enough to climb and glissade
approach_variants.notes:
From the Marble Mountain Sno-Park at about 2,700-2,800 ft, follow the Swift Creek Trail #244 north into forest, marked in winter by blue diamond blazes on the trees. It climbs steadily through timber for roughly 2 miles to about 3,700-3,750 ft, breaking out of the trees near Chocolate Falls on Swift Creek.

Just above the falls, cross to the WEST side of Swift Creek. This ford can be swollen with meltwater in spring or after a warm spell, and the crossing point and its sign are often buried in winter snowpack.

Above treeline the route enters the open barren Worm Flows lava and mudflow terrain. Wooden posts mark the line from about 3,700 to roughly 4,800 ft; above that the posts thin out and occasional cairns, plus wands placed by parties, mark broad ridges and open slopes. The route follows Worm Flow Ridge past an old seismic monitoring station near 6,200 ft, then up snow and scree to merge with the summer Monitor Ridge line at about 7,400 ft, and roughly 850 ft more to the crater rim.

A Sno-Park permit is required to park in the winter months. This is the standard winter and spring access because the summer trailhead on the far side is snow-gated.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THREE HARD MARKERS, IN ORDER, AND THEY WORK BECAUSE THEY ARE OBJECTS RATHER THAN DESCRIPTIONS OF SLOPE — which matters here, since snow buries everything else.

ONE: CHOCOLATE FALLS, at about 3,700-3,750 ft, where the trail breaks out of the trees. You cross to the west side of Swift Creek JUST ABOVE THE FALLS. In winter the crossing point and its sign are usually under snow, so treat the falls themselves as the marker and never a sign.

TWO: WOODEN POSTS, from about 3,700 to about 4,800 ft. Above 4,800 they thin to cairns and wands.

THREE: THE OLD SEISMIC MONITORING STATION near 6,200 ft on Worm Flow Ridge. This is the last hard object on the whole route and the best single confirmation you are on the ridge and not on one of the broad open slopes beside it.

THE NEGATIVE THAT CATCHES PARTIES LOW: if you have crossed Swift Creek and are STILL IN TREES, you crossed too low — below the falls. Regain the east bank and keep climbing to the treeline break.

THE MERGE AT ABOUT 7,400 FT IS THE LAST CHECK: from there you are on the summer Monitor Ridge line and it is roughly 850 ft to the rim.

THE MOST IMPORTANT FINDING ON THIS ROUTE IS ABOUT COMING DOWN, NOT GOING UP. Whiteout wrong-drainage descents are the documented failure here. From the rim the correct line is back down WORM FLOW RIDGE — a ridge, not a gully. Do not descend into a gully because it is going downhill; and record your bearings on the way up while you can still see the ridge you are on.
hazards: Whiteout descents into the wrong drainage — the documented failure mode on this route
Avalanche terrain on loaded slopes and in gully bottoms after new snow or wind loading
Cornice collapse and unstable footing at the crater rim
A Swift Creek ford that can run fast with meltwater and whose crossing point is buried in winter
High wind exposure across the open upper mountain
No reliable water above Chocolate Falls

approach_variants.name: Conrad Meadows and the South Fork Tieton to Klickton Divide
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Conrad Meadows and South Fork Tieton trailhead at road's end, about 4,044 ft, reached by the Tieton Reservoir road and then the South Fork Tieton road off the highway west of Naches. The last several miles are gravel.

Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows, crossing Conrad Creek, into the Goat Rocks Wilderness and on toward Surprise Lake and Warm Lake. From there climb southwest to gain Klickton Divide near Point 6,882, then follow the ridge northwest toward the summit, mixing snow and rock with Gilbert in view most of the way.

An alternative from the same trailhead crosses the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle east of the summit, drops onto the Meade, and climbs it — now largely persistent snowfields rather than a crevassed glacier — to a rock outcrop below the final pitch.

This is a long day: roughly 20 miles round trip with real gain, and limited water late in a dry season.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
GAINING KLICKTON DIVIDE IN THE RIGHT PLACE IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM, AND EVERYTHING BEFORE IT IS TRAIL.

You leave the trail beyond Warm Lake and climb SOUTHWEST to gain the divide near POINT 6,882. From there the ridge runs NORTHWEST to the peak. Two directions, in that order: southwest to gain, northwest to follow. Getting the second one wrong walks you away from the mountain along the same ridge.

THE POSITIVE THAT MAKES THIS A GENEROUS ROUTE IN CLEAR WEATHER, AND A HARSH ONE IN CLOUD: once you are on the divide, GILBERT IS IN VIEW ALMOST THE WHOLE WAY. If you cannot see the peak from the ridge you are either not on the divide or the day has closed in, and in the second case the ridge crest itself is the handrail.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS A NOTCH, AND THERE IS ONLY ONE. The route tops out with a steep snow and scree slope and then a SHORT, LOOSE CLASS 3 SCRAMBLE THROUGH A NOTCH to the true summit. Short is the operative word: the summit is immediately above the notch. If you have gone through a gap and the ground keeps rising well beyond it, you are at the wrong gap.

THE NEGATIVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM ITS SIBLING ON THE SAME PEAK: this line goes ONTO THE RIDGE. The other route from this trailhead goes UNDER the peak — across the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle, then onto the Meade. If you find yourself roping up for glacier travel before you have been on a ridge, you are on that one instead.

SELF-ARREST IS PART OF THE BASE FINDING HERE, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: the snowfield below the summit is steep enough that the route assumes you can hold a slip on it. Arriving without an axe is a reason to turn round at the divide.
hazards: A steep summit snowfield requiring solid self-arrest
Loose rock on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk between parties climbing close together
