Receding glaciers that can still hide crevasses and moats early season
A long, remote round trip of roughly 20 miles with limited water in a dry year
Ridge navigation that depends on visibility once off the trail

approach_variants.name: Conrad Meadows to the north side, the Conrad Glacier and the 7,200 ft saddle
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; rated for summer and fall and not recommended in spring or winter conditions
approach_variants.notes:
From the South Tieton Creek and Conrad Meadows trailhead, approach the north side of the peak and ascend the EAST side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, traverse onto the Meade Glacier, then finish over boulders, scree and a summit snowfield.

The Conrad is the more active of the peak's two small glaciers, so this line wants a rope, a harness and a crevasse-rescue kit rather than just an axe and crampons.

Descent reverses the traverse: back over the saddle and down the Conrad to Conrad Meadows. It is normally done over two or more days given the long approach through the drainage and the talus.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO GLACIERS WITH ONE SADDLE BETWEEN THEM. THAT SEQUENCE IS THE ROUTE AND IT IS THE TEST.

You climb the EAST side of the CONRAD GLACIER to a saddle at about 7,200 ft, and from that saddle you TRAVERSE ONTO A SECOND GLACIER — the Meade — before any of the summit ground. Glacier, saddle, glacier, then boulders, scree and a summit snowfield, in that order.

THE NEGATIVE AT THE SADDLE IS THE ONE WORTH CARRYING: IF YOU REACH A SADDLE AND THE GROUND BEYOND IT IS BOULDERS AND SCREE WITH NO SECOND GLACIER, YOU ARE ON THE WRONG SADDLE. This route's saddle opens onto ice. A saddle that opens onto rock belongs to the ridge line, which is the peak's other route from the same trailhead.

THE ELEVATION IS A CROSS-CHECK RATHER THAN A MARKER: about 7,200 ft. Well above that and you have climbed the glacier past its col; well below and you are still on the apron.

WHICH SIDE OF THE GLACIER MATTERS AND IT IS EASY TO GET WRONG IN THE DARK: the EAST side of the Conrad. Drifting west takes you up the glacier's other flank and away from the saddle.

THE APPROACH-SIDE FINDING: this route comes at the peak from the NORTH. If you have climbed onto a long ridge with the peak in view along it, you are on the Klickton Divide line instead — a fine route, a different day, and it does not need a rope.
hazards: Glacier travel on the Conrad, the more active of the peak's two glaciers
Loose rock, scree and boulder terrain below the summit
A long approach through the Conrad Creek drainage and talus
Not recommended in spring or winter conditions
A traverse between two glaciers with the same ground to reverse on the way out

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flats and the Goat Ledges traverse to the black prow
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the ledges are dry
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat trailhead in the Chambers Lake area on the west side of the Goat Rocks, at about 4,650 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Hike Snowgrass Trail #96 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft along Goat Creek to Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow used as base camp.

From camp, head cross-country and scramble east across the Goat Ledges and Goat Ribs — a series of rock ribs and shallow gullies — at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft toward Gilbert Peak. This is often combined with Old Snowy and Ives in a single traverse day.

A lower variation holds a consistent traverse elevation of about 7,500 ft, which reduces exposure to rockfall knocked down by other parties.

The route is regarded by some as loose and dangerous. Careful route-finding along the correct band and on goat paths is what makes it a reasonable class 4 passage rather than a bad one.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WHITE BAND IS THE ROUTE. THAT IS THE ENTIRE FINDING AND IT IS A COLOUR TEST, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVES BAD LIGHT.

On the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft there is a band of SOLID, ABRASIVE, WHITE PYROCLASTIC AGGREGATE. It points at a NOTCH BEHIND A PROMINENT DARK ROCK TOWER — the black prow. So there are two objects to find and they are opposite colours: a white band and a dark tower, with the notch behind the tower.

THE NEGATIVE IS TACTILE AND IT TELLS YOU IMMEDIATELY, WITHOUT A VIEW: THE WHITE BAND IS SOLID AND ABRASIVE. THE ROCK ABOVE IT AND BELOW IT IS LOOSE. If the holds are moving under your hands you are off the band — traverse back to the white rather than pressing on.

HOLD YOUR HEIGHT AT ABOUT 7,500 FT. Drifting HIGH is worse than drifting low: it puts you above the band and above other parties, in the position that generates the rockfall this traverse is notorious for. The low variation is a deliberate choice, not a mistake.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS THE NOTCH BEHIND THE BLACK PROW. Everything before it is traversing; the class 4 finish begins there. If you are scrambling steeply and you have not passed a dark tower, you have started up too early.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the traverse ends at the peak. If the ribs and gullies keep coming and you have not found a white band pointing anywhere, you are on the wrong tier of the mountain — go back to a rib you can identify and re-find the band, rather than gaining height to look.
hazards: Significant rockfall on the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse, worst with parties stacked at different elevations
Loose andesite, pyroclastic breccia and tuff throughout the upper mountain
Steep, insecure sections approaching the summit block even in dry late-season conditions
Route-finding failure — the whole route depends on correctly identifying the white aggregate band
A class 4 downclimb through the notch on the way back, on the same loose ground

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Trail, the PCT junction and the Old Snowy to Ives col
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul through mid-Sep, once the crest and shaded gullies have melted out
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snowgrass trailhead, also called Berry Patch, at about 4,600 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Follow Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; it drops slightly to cross Goat Creek on a plank crossing around the 2-mile mark, which is the only real water crossing and a reliable source.

Climb through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower and then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft, about 4 miles in — a broad wildflower meadow with good camping and small creeks, the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue a further 0.3 to 0.5 mile to the PCT junction at roughly 6,700-7,100 ft.

Leave the PCT and head off-trail northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread and only occasional cairns, toward the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak. The talus is unconsolidated and shifts underfoot.

Snowfields linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July — this basin can hold 25 to 40 ft of winter snowpack — so an axe is worth carrying for early and mid-season attempts.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN OLD SNOWY AND IVES IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU GET TO IT BY LEAVING A TRAIL, NOT BY FOLLOWING ONE.

Leave the PCT at the junction area, roughly 6,700-7,100 ft, and go off-trail NORTHEAST up talus. There is no tread. Occasional cairns are the only marks. If you are still on maintained trail you have not started the route.

YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT THE COL BECAUSE YOU ARE BETWEEN TWO PEAKS at about 7,250 ft — Old Snowy behind you, Ives ahead. A high point on one side only is not the col.

THE BUMP IS THE TRAP AND IT IS COUNTABLE: from the col the ridge crosses a ROUNDED INTERMEDIATE HIGH POINT before you reach the true summit block. THAT BUMP IS NOT THE SUMMIT. If you have not passed one rounded bump, you have not reached the summit block, whatever the ground in front of you looks like.

THE BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE IS A NOTCH BETWEEN TWO ROCK OUTCROPS, reached by a boot path up scree. And here is the test that settles it beyond doubt, because it is the opposite of what you expect at a summit block: ABOVE THE NOTCH IS A SHORT CLIFF BAND, AND THE ROUTE GOES DOWN FIRST. You downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face, then scramble about 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock to easy ground and the summit.

SO: IF THE LINE IN FRONT OF YOU ONLY GOES UP, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG NOTCH. Having to lose a little height at the notch is the confirmation.

DESCENT FINDING WORTH MAKING BEFORE YOU START: dropping straight southwest off the col into the basin is faster and is the loosest ground on the mountain. Traversing back over Old Snowy and down its established south-ridge path avoids the worst of it.
hazards: Loose, unconsolidated talus and scree with higher consequence on the descent
Chossy volcanic andesite on the summit south face
An exposed narrow ledge traverse below the summit, reached by downclimbing
Lingering snowfields and a moat crossing near the col into July
Off-trail route-finding with no maintained summit path
Exposure to afternoon thunderstorms on an open crest

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flat, the PCT north, and the unmarked climbers' path to the south ridge
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-Jul through Sep, most reliable in August
approach_variants.notes:
From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead at about 4,600 ft at the end of the forest road, start on Trail 96. It climbs gently through forest roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old bypass trail — stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line.

Around 2.4 to 2.6 miles you reach the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right, the last easy water before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek; there is no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except in heavy snowmelt.

Just beyond the ford at about 3.9-4 miles and 6,400 ft the trail breaks into the open heather meadows of Snowgrass Flat. Camping is prohibited within the flat itself under wilderness regulations; parties camp at designated sites above or below it.

Continue past the two trail junctions to the PCT at roughly 7,100 ft and turn right, north. Follow the PCT about 1.8 miles across rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill below Old Snowy's south ridge.

Round trip is roughly 15.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain, typically 8.5 to 9.5 hours car to car. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm before driving.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TURN OFF THE PCT IS UNMARKED, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING ON THIS ROUTE YOU CAN GET WRONG.

THE TEST THAT WORKS IN FOG IS ABOUT MOTION, NOT LANDMARKS: the PCT here is SIDEHILLING — traversing across the slope. The climbers' path is THE FIRST THING THAT TURNS UPHILL AND STOPS CONTOURING, branching right, east, toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's south ridge. Take the first thing that climbs.

THE NEGATIVE IS EQUALLY MECHANICAL: IF THE PCT STARTS DESCENDING ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE TURN. Go back; do not climb straight up from where you noticed.

DISTANCE CROSS-CHECK: about 1.8 miles north of the Trail 96 junction at 7,100 ft, and the path switchbacks steeply for about half a mile from where you leave the trail.

SECOND MARKER, AND IT SITS BEFORE THE TURN RATHER THAN AFTER IT: a persistent SNOWFIELD on the PCT below the summit lingers into July and is a well-documented trouble spot on the exposed sidehill traverse. Meeting it means the turn is still ahead of you. It is firmest and safest crossed in the morning.

A SOFT CONFIRMATION AT THE SADDLE, WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS VISIBLE FROM A DISTANCE: many parties stash trekking poles there for the scramble. A cache of poles on a rocky saddle is a good sign you are at the right one.

BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE: the last few hundred feet to the summit is Class 2-3 hands-and-feet on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rock knocked down by parties above is the hazard, so do not stack directly below other climbers.

AND A NEGATIVE THAT IS ABOUT VISIBILITY RATHER THAN GROUND: once you leave the PCT there is no maintained tread. Poor visibility is the recorded route-finding difficulty on this peak, and the honest response is to turn round at the PCT rather than to search for the spur.
hazards: An unmarked, easily missed turn off the PCT — the route's one real navigation problem
A persistent snowfield on the PCT traverse below the summit, firm and icy in early morning
Loose rock and talus on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk to climbers below
High wind and lightning exposure on an open crest, with common afternoon thunderstorms
Route-finding difficulty in poor visibility once off the PCT
Unreliable cell coverage throughout the wilderness

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes, Pinnacle Saddle and the scree traverse east to the Castle-Pinnacle col
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for dry rock; the line is scrambled into June and October with snow on the approach
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road, or at the year-round Narada Falls lot when that road is snowed in. Take the signed Pinnacle Peak Trail from the south side of the road; it climbs steadily through forest and subalpine meadow for about 1.3 miles and 1,050 ft to the saddle at about 5,920 ft.

From the saddle, do not climb Pinnacle. Traverse east across Pinnacle's south-facing scree and boulder field, holding roughly 6,000-6,200 ft, about another half mile of cross-country travel to the col between Pinnacle and The Castle.

From the col, scramble onto Castle's south rib, make a short class-3 traverse onto the east flank, and follow the crack-chimney system up and right to a notch beside a natural rock horn. A brief exposed class 3-4 scramble along the summit crest reaches the true summit.

Stevens Canyon Road is gated and closed by snow roughly mid-October to late May or early June.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO SADDLES, AND YOU WANT THE SECOND ONE. That is the whole approach problem and it is countable.

The maintained trail ends at PINNACLE SADDLE at about 5,920 ft — the notch between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak. THAT IS NOT YOUR OBJECTIVE. From there you leave the trail and contour EAST across Pinnacle's south scree at 6,000-6,200 ft to a SECOND col, the one between Pinnacle and The Castle. The Castle's base is there.

THREE WAYS TO BE WRONG, AND EACH IS A DIFFERENT PEAK. Start climbing at the first saddle and you are on PINNACLE. Go west from the first saddle and you are heading for PLUMMER. Stop short on the traverse and you are on Pinnacle's south face rather than at the col.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS ONE FEATURE AND IT IS A HOLE, NOT A FACE: an OBVIOUS CRACK-CHIMNEY SYSTEM on the southeast and east flank, gained after a short class-3 traverse off the south rib. If you are on open face with no continuous crack to follow, you are off it — the easy-5th line is in the chimney.

CONFIRMATION AT THE TOP OF THE PITCH, AND IT IS WORTH FINDING DELIBERATELY ON THE WAY UP BECAUSE YOU WILL WANT IT ON THE WAY DOWN: the chimney ends at a NOTCH BESIDE A NATURAL ROCK HORN. That horn is the rappel anchor. Carry your own webbing rather than trusting tat left there.

THE LAST NEGATIVE, AND IT COSTS PEOPLE THE SUMMIT: THE NOTCH IS NOT THE TOP. The true summit is the NORTHERNMOST block, reached by a short exposed scramble along the crest from the notch. If you have topped out of the chimney and stopped, you are one airy scramble short.
hazards: Exposed, largely unprotected class 3-4 terrain along the summit ridge crest
A short 5th-class pitch with sparse natural protection
Loose volcanic rock on the approach scree traverse and off-route
Residual snow and ice on the shaded traverse into early summer
Rapid afternoon thunderstorm development typical of this range in summer

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes and the Pinnacle traverse to the taller summit spire
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is shared with the standard Southeast Face: from Reflection Lakes at about 4,859 ft, take the Pinnacle Peak Trail 1.3 miles to the saddle, then contour east across Pinnacle's south scree to the base of Castle's southeast side, and scramble up broken third-class ground to reach the base of the summit block.

The climbing itself is short: about two-thirds of the pitch is easier ground, there is one solid cam placement, then three slabby crux moves, a jug pull, and easier climbing to a large belay ledge about 10 ft left of the true summit.

From the belay ledge, traverse climber's right past the true summit to the heavily trafficked top-out shared with the Southeast Face, where slings are typically in place, and make a single short rappel back to the base of the technical section.

Stevens Canyon Road typically opens late May and closes with fall snowfall; Narada Falls is the winter and spring trailhead.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
SAME COL AND SAME BROKEN GROUND AS THE STANDARD ROUTE — SO THE DISCRIMINATOR IS NOT THE WALK IN, IT IS WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU AT THE FOOT OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK.

THIS ROUTE IS A DIHEDRAL ON THE TALLER OF THE SUMMIT SPIRES. THE STANDARD ROUTE IS A CRACK-CHIMNEY. So: A CORNER YOU STEM IS THIS ROUTE. A SLOT YOU GET INSIDE IS THE SOUTHEAST FACE. That single distinction separates a 5.7 with an 5.8 crux from an easy-5th scramble, and it is decided at the ground.

THE ORDERING WITHIN THE PITCH IS THE SECOND CONFIRMATION, AND IT IS COUNTABLE: roughly two-thirds of the pitch is easier climbing, THEN one good cam placement, THEN three slabby crux moves, THEN a jug pull, then easy ground to the ledge. IF THE HARD MOVES COME AT THE VERY START, YOU ARE NOT ON THIS ROUTE. The crux here is high on a short pitch, which is also why a fall from it has consequence — there are ledges below.

THE TOP-OUT TEST IS THE ONE THAT SETTLES IT AFTERWARDS: this pitch finishes on a LARGE BELAY LEDGE ABOUT 10 FT LEFT OF THE TRUE SUMMIT. Topping out level with the summit rather than on it is correct here. You then traverse climber's RIGHT, past the true summit, to reach the shared rappel station.

SO THE NEGATIVE IS: IF YOU TOPPED OUT DIRECTLY AT A SLUNG HORN WITH OLD TAT ON IT, YOU CLIMBED THE STANDARD SOUTHEAST FACE. That horn is the shared descent anchor, not this route's finish.

ONE PRACTICAL FINDING FOR THE APPROACH SCRAMBLE ITSELF: the third-class ground below the block is exposed enough that a fall has real consequence. It is the part of this outing that is soloed by everyone and guarded by nobody.
hazards: Exposed third-class scrambling with real fall potential just to reach the base of the pitch
A crux high on a short pitch, above ledges
Early-season snow and ice on the traverse from the saddle
Loose rock on the approach scramble and gully
Afternoon thunderstorms and exposure on the summit block and connecting ridge

approach_variants.name: Longmire, the Nisqually suspension bridge and the Eagle Peak Trail to the saddle
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the saddle can be corniced with lingering snow into June
approach_variants.notes:
The Eagle Peak trailhead is about 300 ft past the suspension bridge on the east side of the Nisqually River at Longmire, which is normally reachable year-round.

The maintained trail — about 7.2 miles round trip and nearly 3,000 ft of gain — climbs steeply through old-growth forest for roughly two miles to a stream crossing, continues about a mile to a meadow, then steepens over rocky ground for a final half mile to Eagle Peak Saddle at about 5,700-5,720 ft, where the maintained trail ends.

The saddle is exposed, with cliff edges that hold cornices into early summer. Everything above it is scrambling on a climbers' path.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MAINTAINED TRAIL ENDS AT THE SADDLE, AND THE SADDLE IS NOT THE SUMMIT. Eagle Peak Saddle is about 5,700 ft; the summit is 5,958 ft, roughly a quarter mile east along the ridge. The trail ending is the start of the route, not the end of it.

THE BASE OF THE TECHNICAL GROUND IS A ROCK STEP WITH LOOSE HOLDS, reached by following the path EAST from the saddle. That step is class 4 and it is harder coming down than going up.

THE MOST USEFUL FINDING HERE IS ABOUT THE BYPASS, BECAUSE MOST PARTIES WANT IT AND IT IS BEHIND THEM BY THE TIME THEY NEED IT: GO LEFT 100 TO 200 FEET INTO A SHORT CLASS 3 GULLY, climb it to a ledge, and rejoin the main line at the TOP of the rock step. SO IF YOU ARE STANDING UNDER A LOOSE CLASS 4 STEP WONDERING WHETHER IT IS HARDER THAN ADVERTISED, YOU WALKED PAST THE BYPASS ONE TO TWO HUNDRED FEET BACK ON YOUR LEFT.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS ON YOUR LEFT AND THE RULE IS SIMPLE: STAY RIGHT. If the high ground ahead of you is off to the left, that is the false summit, not the top.

THE RIDGE IS EXPOSED ON BOTH SIDES for the whole stretch above the saddle, on uneven ground. Ground that only falls away on one side means you are still on the approach path, not on the crest.

AND ONE THING WORTH FIXING IN YOUR HEAD BEFORE YOU COMMIT, BECAUSE IT IS THE DESCENT THAT CATCHES PEOPLE: the crux step is harder downwards, with a blind foothold. Face outward, pivot right to face into the rock, then step down. Deciding that at the top of it in the rain is too late.
hazards: Exposed terrain at the saddle with cliff edges and cornices into June — falls here are fatal
Loose holds on the class 4 rock step, which most parties should bypass
The crux step is harder to descend than to climb, with a blind foothold
Rockfall between parties on a narrow ridge
Steep meadow avalanche terrain in winter
Wet rock materially increases the scrambling difficulty

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes or Narada Falls, Tatoosh Creek and the debris apron under the north face
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-Jun; most ascents are in winter and spring
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road when it is open, or at Narada Falls in winter and spring when the road is snow-gated — from Narada Falls a short steep climb of about 200 ft through open timber regains the road.

Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face.

From the basin, hike up and across a large TRIANGULAR APRON of avalanche and rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloirs. From the top of that debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft of couloir to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel point.

Roughly 2 to 2.5 miles one-way with about 2,000 ft of gain to the notch, and no water past Tatoosh Creek. The basin and lower couloir cross avalanche terrain, so this is a start-early, read-the-forecast approach.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ON THIS FACE THE THREE COULOIRS ARE: LOVER'S LANE, THE ZIPPER, THE FLY. Learn that order before you leave the car. All three drop onto the same debris apron and on a busy weekend all three have parties on them at once, which means overhead hazard from other people as well as from the mountain.

THE ZIPPER IS THE MIDDLE ONE, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT LEANS LEFT AND SPLITS THE CENTRE OF THE FACE. From the top of the debris cone, angle CLIMBER'S LEFT. If you are working right, you are heading for the Fly.

THE STRONGEST TEST IS WIDTH, AND IT IS A THING YOU FEEL RATHER THAN SEE: THE ZIPPER NARROWS. About 40 ft wide at the base, closing to about 20 ft near the top. THE FLY IS BROAD — 40 to 50 ft — AND IT STAYS BROAD. If the walls are not closing in on you as you gain height, you are in the Fly, one couloir to your right, on easier ground than you came for.

THE SECOND TEST IS COUNTABLE AND IT IS THE ONE THAT SETTLES IT: THE ZIPPER HAS UP TO THREE SHORT STEPS — about 15 ft, then about 8 ft, then a 25 ft crux near the top. The Fly has none worth the name. IF YOU HAVE CLIMBED A THOUSAND FEET OF CONTINUOUS 45-DEGREE SNOW AND MET NO STEP AT ALL, YOU ARE NOT IN THE ZIPPER.

THE TOP-OUT IS AN OBJECT, WHICH IS THE BEST KIND OF CONFIRMATION: A DEAD TREE AT A NOTCH IN THE EAST RIDGE. That tree carries the fixed rappel slings. If you have topped out onto open ridge with no tree, you are on something else — Lover's Lane finishes on the ridge ABOVE this notch, and the Fly finishes at the west-ridge notch.

WHAT THE ANGLE SHOULD DO: build from about 40 degrees to about 45 near the top. It does not exceed that. Ground steeper than 45 sustained means Lover's Lane, which reaches about 60.
hazards: Avalanche terrain in the basin and lower couloir, with both loose-dry and wet-loose problems documented on this aspect
Overhead hazard from other parties — this face is busy on good winter weekends and all three couloirs get climbed at once
Variable ice and mixed conditions in the steps season to season
A rappel that is longer than a single 60 m rope doubled, and rope-snag potential on rock features
Short winter days leaving little margin for retreat
Rockfall and spindrift funnelling into the couloir from above

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes or Narada Falls to the debris apron, then the rightmost couloir
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-Jun
approach_variants.notes:
Shared approach with the Zipper: from Reflection Lakes when the road is open, or from Narada Falls when it is gated, walk the road briefly and drop south into the basin toward Tatoosh Creek, then climb the debris triangle to the base of the couloir system. Roughly 2 miles with about 2,000 ft of gain; the approach usually takes 1.5 to 2 hours from the road to the couloir base.

The Fly is a broad couloir about 40 to 50 ft wide, predominantly snow at around 45 degrees, and is the easiest objective on the north face with fewer technical sections than the Zipper. The most efficient line follows the obvious broad gully, trending slightly right as you gain height.

The runout zone at the base is avalanche-prone, so stable snow is essential.

From the top at the west-ridge notch, most parties continue round onto the South Face and descend the standard third and fourth class gully rather than reversing the couloir.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT: LOVER'S LANE, THE ZIPPER, THE FLY. THE FLY IS THE RIGHTMOST, AND IT IS THE BROADEST.

BREADTH IS THE TEST AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE YOU NEED AT THE BOTTOM: 40 to 50 ft wide, and IT STAYS THAT WIDE. IF THE COULOIR NARROWS TOWARD ABOUT 20 FT AND STARTS PUTTING SHORT ICE STEPS IN FRONT OF YOU, YOU ARE IN THE ZIPPER, ONE TO YOUR LEFT, ON HARDER GROUND THAN YOU CAME FOR.

THE SECOND TEST IS WHAT YOUR HANDS ARE DOING. This is the easiest line on the face — predominantly snow at about 45 degrees with no crux step. IF YOU ARE SWINGING TWO TOOLS INTO ICE, YOU ARE NOT ON THE FLY.

TREND SLIGHTLY RIGHT AS YOU GAIN HEIGHT. That is the route's own shape, and drifting left at the base is exactly how parties end up in the Zipper.

THE TOP-OUT NAMES THE COULOIR RETROSPECTIVELY, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING IF YOU HAD ANY DOUBT ON THE WAY UP: the Fly finishes at the WEST-RIDGE NOTCH. The Zipper finishes at a notch in the EAST ridge, at a DEAD TREE carrying rappel slings. If you topped out at a tree, you climbed the Zipper.

A NEGATIVE THAT IS ABOUT PEOPLE RATHER THAN GROUND, AND IT IS SPECIFIC TO THIS FACE: on a good winter weekend all three couloirs carry parties at the same time, and a documented near-miss involved thirteen climbers and skiers spread across the three. Being able to see other parties is not confirmation you are in the right gully — it is a reason to watch what comes down.

WHAT THE ANGLE SHOULD DO: about 40 to 45 degrees for the main gully, easing to 30-35 in the last few hundred feet to the ridge. It does not steepen near the top.
hazards: An avalanche-prone runout zone at the base of the couloir
Overhead hazard from parties on the neighbouring couloirs and from rockfall out of the walls once the sun hits
Variable snow and ice conditions season to season
Short winter days
Wet-loose avalanche activity documented on the slopes below the peak

approach_variants.name: Narada Falls, under Denman Peak, and the first steep avalanche funnel
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-May
approach_variants.notes:
Begin at the Narada Falls parking area, which is plowed and open year-round. Travel on skis or snowshoes along the closed Reflection Lakes road, then traverse steep hillsides under Denman Peak toward Lane Peak's base, turning sharply uphill at the first steep avalanche funnel to reach the base of the couloir.

The route is a north-facing couloir immediately climber's left of the Zipper, with two or three steeper ice and mixed sections needing screws or pickets, and an upper couloir that steepens to about 60 degrees before topping out on the ridge above the Zipper.

From the top, the standard move is a rappel of more than 100 ft — a double rope is recommended — down into the adjacent Zipper couloir, then either downclimb the remaining Zipper snow or continue over to the standard South Face line and the Lane-Denman saddle.

The approach traverse is itself avalanche terrain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT: LOVER'S LANE, THE ZIPPER, THE FLY. THIS IS THE LEFTMOST — IMMEDIATELY CLIMBER'S LEFT OF THE ZIPPER.

THE APPROACH TEST IS A COUNT, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT WORKS ON A SKI TRACK IN THE DARK: traversing under DENMAN PEAK toward Lane's base, you turn sharply uphill AT THE FIRST STEEP AVALANCHE FUNNEL YOU MEET. FIRST, not second. IF YOU HAVE PASSED ONE FUNNEL AND CARRIED ON TO ANOTHER, YOU ARE AT THE ZIPPER.

THE CLIMBING TEST IS ANGLE, AND IT IS DECISIVE BECAUSE THIS ROUTE IS THE STEEPEST OF THE THREE: the upper couloir reaches about 60 degrees, with two or three steeper ice and mixed sections below it that want screws. IF NOTHING HAS EXCEEDED ABOUT 45 DEGREES, YOU ARE IN THE ZIPPER OR THE FLY.

THE TOP-OUT TEST IS THE DEFINITIVE ONE, AND IT IS UNIQUE TO THIS ROUTE: LOVER'S LANE FINISHES ON THE RIDGE ABOVE THE ZIPPER, AND THE STANDARD DESCENT IS A RAPPEL OF MORE THAN 100 FT FROM THAT RIDGE INTO THE ZIPPER ITSELF. SO IF YOU CAN LOOK DOWN INTO A NEIGHBOURING COULOIR FROM WHERE YOU TOPPED OUT, YOU ARE ON LOVER'S LANE. If instead you topped out at a DEAD TREE IN A NOTCH with slings on it, you climbed the Zipper.

PLAN THE ROPE BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE CAR, BECAUSE THE TOP OF THIS ROUTE IS THE WRONG PLACE TO FIND OUT: the rappel is usually longer than 100 ft, so a single 70 m doubled will not reach cleanly in a normal year. Two ropes, or a very deliberate plan for downclimbing the first section.

AND THE THING THAT MAKES THIS ROUTE'S DESCENT DIFFERENT FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS': you do not descend your own line. You rappel into somebody else's, which is a good reason to know where parties on the Zipper are before you pull the rope.
hazards: Avalanche exposure on the approach traverse beneath Denman Peak
Steep sustained ice and mixed ground that can be harder than rated depending on conditions
A rappel that transfers the party into the adjacent Zipper couloir, with rockfall and rope-pull consequences for anyone below
A rappel usually longer than a single 70 m rope doubled
Short winter days on a north aspect

approach_variants.name: Tatoosh Creek, the timber band and the Lane-Denman saddle
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road, open roughly late May through mid-October, or from Narada Falls when the road is gated — from Narada Falls a short steep climb of about 200 ft through open timber gains the road.

Walk the road roughly half a mile to where it bends sharply and begins heading east. Leave the pavement there and drop south through sparse open forest to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft, losing a couple of hundred feet. Cross the creek — a rock-hop most of the season, more involved at peak snowmelt — and angle up a broad talus slope of about 250 vertical feet.

At the top of the talus, continue up through trees STAYING RIGHT of a short cliff band. Roughly 700 ft above the creek, near 5,200 ft, you break out of the trees onto open slopes and continue to the broad Lane-Denman saddle at about 5,440 ft.

From the saddle, turn right and climb moderate open ground to the gully weakness in the southeast face. Follow it up, trending left near the top for a final short scramble to the summit. Round trip is a bit over 3 miles with roughly 1,400-1,500 ft of gain, and no water past Tatoosh Creek.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN FROM THE THREE COULOIRS, AND THE MISTAKE IT INVITES IS WALKING INTO THE NORTH-FACE BASIN WITH THE ICE CLIMBERS. The single clearest separator is Tatoosh Creek: THE COULOIR ROUTES STAY LOW IN THE BASIN. THIS ROUTE CROSSES THE CREEK AND CLIMBS THE OTHER SIDE.

THE SEQUENCE, EACH ITEM A CHECK, IN ORDER:
1. Off the road at the 90-degree bend, south, down to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. CROSS IT.
2. Up a talus slope of about 250 vertical feet.
3. Into trees, STAYING RIGHT OF A SHORT CLIFF BAND. This is the one place on the route where an error commits you to bad ground — the timber is brushy and drifting left cliffs you out. If you find yourself under rock in the trees, traverse back right before gaining more height.
4. Break out of the trees about 700 ft above the creek, near 5,200 ft.
5. Arrive at the broad LANE-DENMAN SADDLE at about 5,440 ft.

THE SADDLE TEST IS A COUNT OF PEAKS: you should have HIGH GROUND ON BOTH SIDES OF YOU — Lane on one hand, Denman on the other. A col with only one peak above it is not this saddle.

FROM THE SADDLE, TURN RIGHT — WEST. DENMAN IS THE OTHER WAY, and it is an easy mistake in cloud because both directions climb.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS THE OBVIOUS GULLY WEAKNESS IN THE SOUTHEAST FACE, and it is the feature the route is named for. THE CONFIRMATION INSIDE IT IS AN OBJECT: a STURDY TREE roughly 200 ft up the climbing, which is the main anchor and the rappel point. Reaching a good tree in the gully means you are in the right gully.

LAST: trend LEFT near the top for the final short scramble. Plentiful holds, minimal exposure — if it feels serious, you have drifted out of the gully onto the face.
hazards: Cliffing out in the brushy timber band if the line drifts left of the cliff band
Loose rock and rockfall in the narrow summit gully, especially with parties above
Exposed fourth-class moves just below the true summit
Tatoosh Creek can be difficult during high spring runoff
Afternoon thunderstorms are common over this range in summer
Inconsistent glissade conditions in the gully once it melts out

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle, then east to the chute beside the western prominence
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
From the signed Pinnacle Saddle trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, across from the Reflection Lakes parking area, follow the maintained trail south. It switchbacks up through subalpine forest and meadow, passes beneath cliffs around 0.9 mile, and gains about 1,000-1,050 ft over 1.3 miles to the saddle at 5,920 ft between Pinnacle and Plummer.

At the saddle, leave the maintained tread and follow the unmaintained boot path roughly a quarter mile toward the western side of Pinnacle's south face, to the base of the obvious ascent chute.

From there, hike and scramble a mix of scree and loose rock along or below the ridge on the most-travelled line to a chute east of the western prominence. The chute climbs on increasingly steep, exposed but better-cleaned rock to top out near the summit.

Stevens Canyon Road is gated in winter and spring, typically opening around late May and closing at the first significant snowfall.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PINNACLE SADDLE YOU GO EAST. PLUMMER PEAK IS WEST, AND THE BOOT PATHS FORK AT THE SADDLE, SO THIS IS A DECISION AND NOT A DEFAULT.

THE BASE IS DEFINED BY TWO OBJECTS AND THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THEM: A WESTERN PROMINENCE, AND AN OBVIOUS CHUTE IMMEDIATELY EAST OF IT. About a quarter mile of boot path from the saddle. If you cannot identify a prominence, you cannot identify the chute — go on until you can see one, rather than starting up the first weakness.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH CARRYING: THE CORRECT CHUTE GETS BETTER AS IT GETS STEEPER. The lower approach is scree and choss; the chute itself is progressively steeper AND progressively better-cleaned rock. SO IF THE ROCK IS GETTING LOOSER AS YOU CLIMB, YOU ARE IN THE WRONG GULLY. That is the reverse of what most loose volcanic scrambles do, and it is the most reliable signal on this route.

STAY ON THE MOST-TRAVELLED LINE ON THE APPROACH SCREE. There are multiple possible lines; the worst loose rock is off the beaten one.

A CLEAN NEGATIVE ABOUT HARDWARE: THERE IS NO FIXED PROTECTION ANYWHERE ON THIS ROUTE. Only natural options exist — a few horns and trees near the top that can be slung. IF YOU FIND BOLTS, A PITON, OR A FIXED STATION, YOU ARE ON ONE OF THE PEAK'S ROPED LINES, NOT ON THE SCRAMBLE. The East Ridge, in particular, has an old piton and a fixed rappel anchor.

DOWNCLIMB PLANNING AS PART OF THE FINDING: the class 4 section is more hazardous in descent than ascent because the rock is loose. Parties who intend to back off do it with an improvised sling on a horn or a tree near the top — worth spotting one on the way up.
hazards: Loose rock and choss on the scree approach and lower chute
No fixed protection on the class 4 section; only natural horns and trees near the top
Increasing exposure in the upper chute as the rock steepens
Loose rock is more dangerous descending than ascending
Afternoon thunderstorms on a fully exposed south face

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle, then east behind Pinnacle to the Castle-Pinnacle col
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
From the Reflection Lakes trailhead, follow the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail 1.3 miles and about 1,000-1,050 ft to the Pinnacle-Plummer saddle. From there, continue on unmaintained boot path east and behind Pinnacle toward Castle Peak to reach the Castle-Pinnacle col. Trip reports put that segment at roughly 2 to 3 hours and about 1,500 ft of gain.

The east ridge rises directly from the col. Pitch 1 scrambles mostly fourth-class ground to a belay ledge at a large dead tree. Pitch 2 is the crux: blocky mid-fifth climbing with an exposed traverse to a sandy belay bench carrying a fixed rappel anchor down the south face. Pitch 3 is mellow ground to the true summit, often simul-climbed or soloed.

Loose rock and scree are a serious and repeatedly noted concern throughout.

Descent is either the rappel off the pitch-2 bench down the south face, or over the summit and down the standard south-side scramble to Pinnacle Saddle — the second is only sensible if the leader already knows that line.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE CASTLE-PINNACLE COL, NOT PINNACLE SADDLE, AND THE TWO ARE HALF A MILE AND ONE PEAK APART. The maintained trail ends at the saddle; you keep going EAST, on boot path, behind Pinnacle, toward The Castle.

WHEN YOU ARE AT THE COL YOU CANNOT MISS THE ROUTE: THE EAST RIDGE RISES DIRECTLY FROM IT. If you are at a col and no defined ridge crest goes up from it toward Pinnacle, you are at the wrong col.

THE CONFIRMATIONS ARE OBJECTS, IN ORDER, AND EACH IS ONE OF A KIND ON THIS ROUTE:
PITCH 1 — mostly fourth-class scrambling ending at a belay ledge AT A LARGE DEAD TREE. One tree, one ledge. If you have run out a full pitch and found no tree, you are not on the ridge.
PITCH 2 — blocky mid-fifth climbing with an exposed traverse, an OLD PITON partway up, ending on a SANDY BELAY BENCH with a FIXED RAPPEL ANCHOR dropping the south face. Piton, then sand, then an anchor, in that order. Treat the piton as a backup clip and not as protection.
PITCH 3 — mellow ground to the true summit.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS AT THE COL, BECAUSE TWO PEAKS SHARE IT: The Castle's own route also starts here. IF WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU IS A CRACK-CHIMNEY SYSTEM ON A ROCK FLANK RATHER THAN A DEFINED RIDGE CREST, YOU ARE FACING THE CASTLE AND YOU NEED TO TURN AROUND — Pinnacle is the other side of the col.

THE SECOND NEGATIVE, FOR PARTIES WHO CAME UP THE PEAK'S OTHER LINE BEFORE: this route does not start from Pinnacle Saddle and does not touch the south-face chute. If you are on scree below the south face you are on the scramble route.

ROPE PLANNING AS PART OF THE FINDING: the rappel off the pitch-2 bench is rope-stretching, and a 60 m rope may not reach the ground depending on where the anchor sits. Know that before you commit to it as your descent.
hazards: Loose rock and scree throughout — a serious and repeatedly noted concern on this route
An old, unreliable piton at the pitch-2 crux traverse
A rope-stretching rappel that a 60 m rope may not complete
Exposure on the pitch-2 traverse with sparse natural protection
Rockfall onto the col and onto anyone approaching The Castle from the same place

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle and the south gully
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow or verglas can linger in the gully into July in a cold year
approach_variants.notes:
From the Pinnacle Peak trailhead — a signed unnumbered trail directly across Stevens Canyon Road from the Reflection Lakes pullouts at about 4,860 ft — the maintained trail climbs at a steady, fairly steep grade through sparse subalpine forest. Around half a mile you get the first partial view of Rainier through the trees, then the trail switchbacks up through meadow. At about 1.25-1.3 miles and roughly 1,000-1,050 ft you top out at Pinnacle Saddle near 5,900-5,920 ft, where the maintained trail ends and the view opens south.

Carry water from the car; there is no reliable source on the trail or in the gully except lingering snowmelt early in the season.

Past the saddle the route becomes an unmaintained climbers' path. The rock is old, variable-quality lava flow — solid in places and rotten in others — so test holds and watch for loose blocks with parties above or below.

This is a fully exposed ridge with quick-building afternoon thunderstorms in summer; plan to be off the summit by early afternoon.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PINNACLE SADDLE, THE PEAK IS EAST. Pinnacle is the peak east of the saddle and Plummer is the peak west of it, and the boot paths fork there. GOING WEST FROM THE SADDLE PUTS YOU ON PLUMMER — a different summit, and a party can climb it believing it is this one.

SO: CONTOUR OR SCRAMBLE EAST into the gully system on the south and southeast face.

THE SEQUENCE INSIDE THE GULLY IS WHAT TELLS YOU IT IS THE RIGHT ONE, AND ONE ITEM IN IT IS UNEXPECTED ENOUGH TO BE A REAL TEST: it starts as class 2 scree and blocky steps, steepens into sustained class 3 with real exposure over its upper third, THEN WORKS THROUGH A BAND OF TREES, then a final short scramble to the summit block. TREES HIGH IN THE GULLY ARE THE CONFIRMATION. A gully with no tree band in it is not this one.

MULTIPLE GULLY LINES EXIST HERE, AND THE CORRECT ONE IS THE MOST TRAVELLED. The negative is tactile: if you are dislodging blocks with every step, you are off the beaten line. Loose rock is worst away from it.

THE EARLY-SEASON NEGATIVE IS A TURN-AROUND, NOT A ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM, AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: snow or verglas in this gully turns easy scrambling into a slip you cannot stop, on ground with no protection. That is the condition to go home on rather than to push through with an axe you are not going to be able to use in a chimney.

ONE MORE THING AT THE SADDLE THAT IS NOT A NAVIGATION MARKER BUT WILL BE THE FIRST THING YOU MEET: mountain goats here are habituated and come for the salt. They are not a sign you are on route.
hazards: Loose, unstable rock through the south-facing summit gully
Steep dropoffs and exposure on sections of the maintained trail itself, not only above the saddle
Snow lingering in the summit gully into early or mid summer after the trail has melted out
Rockfall onto parties below on a heavily travelled line
Sudden afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed south Cascades ridge
No water anywhere on the trail or the scramble

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle, the tarn shelf and the north slopes
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; a snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road. The signed Pinnacle Peak Trail leaves the south side of the road, directly across from the largest of the lakes.

The trail climbs moderately through mountain hemlock and Alaska yellow cedar for the first half-mile; around 0.5 mile you get a first partial view of Rainier, and at about 0.6 mile you cross a seasonal cascading creek — the only reliable water on the hike, and dry by late summer in a low-snow year. By 0.7 mile it breaks into open talus and heather below Pinnacle's cliffs and steepens noticeably. Lingering snow on these shaded north-facing switchbacks is the trail's main hazard, since a slip on hard morning snow above the talus can slide a hiker into rock. Around 0.9-1.0 mile the trail passes beneath the cliff bands on Pinnacle's north face, then switchbacks up a short exposed final pitch to Pinnacle Saddle at about 1.25-1.3 miles and roughly 5,920-5,960 ft.

The saddle is the trail's official end and the junction where unmaintained paths fork east toward Denman and The Castle and west toward Plummer.

Stevens Canyon Road is open roughly late May through late October and the small trailhead lot commonly fills by mid-morning on summer weekends.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PINNACLE SADDLE, PLUMMER IS WEST — the opposite direction from Pinnacle, and the paths fork right there.

BUT THE SADDLE IS NOT THE DECISION POINT. THE TARN IS. Here is the sequence, and the middle item is the whole route-finding problem:
1. Continue a short distance PAST the saddle and look for a climbers' path branching RIGHT, west.
2. It crosses a FLAT ROCKY SHELF HOLDING A SEASONAL TARN. The tarn is the marker.
3. AT THAT SHELF A FORK CONTINUES STRAIGHT TOWARD DENMAN PEAK. DO NOT TAKE IT. BEAR LEFT, south and uphill, onto the boot path climbing Plummer's open rocky north slopes.

SO THE ENTIRE PROBLEM REDUCES TO ONE SENTENCE: AT THE TARN, STRAIGHT IS DENMAN AND LEFT IS PLUMMER.

THE NEGATIVE IS A MOTION TEST AND IT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING: IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING LEVEL, OR LOSING HEIGHT, YOU ARE ON THE DENMAN FORK. Plummer's path climbs from the tarn.

THE BASE OF THE HANDS-ON GROUND: the last few hundred feet is class 2-3 with a couple of short hands-on steps, and A FEW WELL-PLACED TREES AID THE FINAL MOVES. Trees on a summit slope at this height are unusual enough to be a confirmation.

THE SUMMIT IS SMALL AND THAT IS THE LAST CHECK — roughly 50 by 15 ft. If you are standing on a broad top, you are on the shoulder below it.

EARLY-SEASON DETAIL THAT IS A REAL FORK RATHER THAN A CAUTION: a snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July. Either kick steps straight up it or skirt LEFT onto the rockier tread. Both rejoin near the top, so neither choice loses the route.
hazards: Lingering snowfield on the steep shaded switchbacks below the saddle, icy in early morning — the most common problem spot
Steep, eroded, loose tread and exposed traverse sections on the upper approach trail
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on an exposed ridge and saddle with no shelter above treeline
Loose rock and thin tread on the final scramble, which feels more exposed descending
Winter avalanche terrain on the peak's slopes
No water past the seasonal creek low on the trail

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake, the northwest gully and Unicorn Col to the summit horn
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; the approach gully holds firm snow through much of July
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lake trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, about 1.5 miles east of Reflection Lakes. The lot holds only about 25 cars and fills by mid-morning on summer weekends.

Follow the maintained Snow Lake Trail through subalpine forest and meadow, past the Bench Lake junction, to Snow Lake at about 1.3-1.5 miles — the last reliable water. Skirt the lake's west and north shore, then leave the maintained tread where a climbers' path breaks off and climbs a steep drainage about half a mile into the large open bowl on Unicorn's northwest side, shared with Foss and West Unicorn.

The basin is loose talus and scree; through much of July the gully above the lake can still hold firm snow, so carry an axe and, in early season, crampons.

From the basin, climb to the saddle on the peak's west side, then traverse and scramble east and around to approach the summit pinnacle from its south side — sustained class 2-3 on talus and blocky rock. About 2.4 miles one-way and 2,397 ft of gain to the base of the summit block, where the roped climbing starts.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HORN IS THE POINT AND THE COL IS NOT. Unicorn Col, the saddle just west of the summit at about 6,400 ft, is where the route-finding stops feeling hard — but the summit is still a traverse away, EAST, and around onto the SOUTH side.

THE TEST AT THE COL IS A SHAPE: the summit block is a FREE-STANDING 50 TO 70 FT HORN, the thing the peak is named for. IF NOTHING IN FRONT OF YOU LOOKS LIKE A DETACHED TOWER, YOU HAVE NOT COME FAR ENOUGH EAST.

THE APPROACH NEGATIVE IS IN THE GULLY AND IT IS THE ONE THAT PUTS PARTIES ON BAD GROUND: aim for the MAIN gully out of the basin above Snow Lake, and AVOID THE STEEP HEADWALLS TO ITS LEFT. If the ground ahead gets steep and rocky rather than staying a talus or snow chute, you have drifted left. Go back down and across rather than pressing up.

THE TRAVERSE NEGATIVE IS ABOUT HEIGHT, NOT DIRECTION: the correct use trail traverses BELOW the cliffs on the south side, and it is easier travel than the loose scree above and below it. If you are scrambling up onto the ridge crest instead of contouring underneath it, you are above the path and on worse rock.

AND THE THING THAT MATTERS MOST AT THE FOOT OF THE HORN: THREE SEPARATE LINES START WITHIN ABOUT 70 FT OF EACH OTHER THERE, and they run from easy fifth class to 5.6. LEFT TO RIGHT THEY ARE: THE ROOF, THE CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK. All three finish at the same slung block, so the only place to get this right is at the bottom. Know which one you came for before you rope up.

DESCENT FINDING, DECIDED BEFORE YOU START UP: most parties rappel the horn rather than downclimb it — a single-rope rappel of about 50 ft down the south side. The traditional anchor is an aging tree at the top of the block; many parties instead sling the rock horn on the south side, which carries slings and rings left by others. Both are climber-built and neither is maintained: inspect and back up before weighting anything. There are two rappel lines off that horn and they land in different places, so confirm which you are on.
hazards: Loose talus and scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out, usually mid-to-late July
Wet-slide and cornice hazard in the northwest gully and bowl in late spring, with documented slide paths off the cliffs above Snow Lake
An exposed step near the top of the summit horn with real air below on the east side
Climber-built rappel anchors of uncertain age, including a tree reported as no longer sound
Afternoon thunderstorms in summer and unreliable cell coverage

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the middle line on the summit horn
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Shared approach with the peak's other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, take the maintained Snow Lake Trail about a mile and roughly 700 ft to Snow Lake, the last water. Skirt the west and north shore; the tread continues a short way over a tree-covered rise before petering out into talus.

Work up and right toward the obvious talus and dirt gully on the peak's northwest side; a climbers' path picks up again on a heather bench near the top of the gully. Follow it into the basin, then climb moraine along the left side of the small permanent snow patch to Unicorn Col just west of the summit. A climbers' path traverses below the cliffs — easier travel than the scree either side — and leads east around the south side to the base of the summit horn.

The climb itself is a single pitch of blocky low-fifth-class climbing, about 40-50 ft, on the south and southeast face, with one fixed piton mid-pitch.

Roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way and about 2,400 ft of gain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ALONG THE FOOT OF THE HORN: THE ROOF, THE CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK. All three start within about 70 ft of each other and all three finish at the same slung block, so the BOTTOM is the only place this can be got right.

THE CLASSIC ROUTE IS THE MIDDLE ONE, AND IT TAKES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST FACE DIRECT — blocky low-fifth climbing straight up, one pitch of about 40-50 ft, with ONE FIXED PITON MID-PITCH. A piton at half height on open face is the positive confirmation.

THE DISTANCE TEST IS THE PRACTICAL ONE AND IT WORKS BY FEEL RATHER THAN BY SIGHT:
  — THE ROOF STARTS ABOUT 20 FT TO YOUR LEFT, at the point where the RIDGELINE MEETS THE BLOCK.
  — OPEN BOOK STARTS ABOUT 50 FT TO YOUR RIGHT, at TWO WIDE, LEFT-LEANING CRACKS.

SO THE TWO NEGATIVES ARE TACTILE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WANT WHEN THE HORN IS IN CLOUD: IF YOU ARE FIGHTING A WIDE AWKWARD CRACK THAT WANTS BIG CAMS, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THIS ROUTE TO THE RIGHT AND YOU ARE ON OPEN BOOK. IF THERE IS A ROOF OVER YOUR HEAD AND YOU ARE IN A GULLY OR CHIMNEY, YOU HAVE GONE LEFT PAST IT AND YOU ARE ON THE ROOF, at 5.6.

CHARACTER TEST: this is blocky face and crack climbing on the OPEN face. Not inside a chimney, not in a wide crack. If you are inside anything, you are on a neighbour.

WHY IT MATTERS: this is the middle grade of the three — 5.4, against Open Book's easy fifth and The Roof's 5.6. Being one line out changes the grade in whichever direction you drifted, on a short pitch above broken ground.

DESCENT DETAIL WORTH SETTLING AT THE TOP RATHER THAN OVER THE EDGE: there are effectively two rappel lines off the summit block, one dropping to the notch and the ground below the horn, the other landing on the snow patch side. A 30 m rope has been reported as just short depending on which one you use and on how open the moat is late season; 40 m removes the guesswork. Use the ROCK HORN — the old bleached snag some older reports mention is no longer sound.
hazards: Loose blocks on the approach scramble to the base of the horn
A short exposed pitch above broken ground where a fall has real consequence
A rappel that may not reach the ground on a 30 m rope, particularly with an open moat late season
An old bleached snag at the top that is no longer a sound anchor
Two different rappel lines off the same block landing in different places

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the rightmost line on the summit horn
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Identical approach to the peak's other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, the maintained trail about a mile and roughly 700 ft to Snow Lake, the last water. Past the lake the tread fades over a wooded rise; work up and right into the talus and dirt gully on the northwest side, where a climbers' path reappears on a heather bench near the top and leads into the basin beneath the summit block. Ascend moraine along the edge of the small basin snowfield to Unicorn Col, then follow the traversing use trail below the cliffs on the south side to the base of the horn.

This route takes the east-facing side of the pinnacle rather than the south face direct, and it is the easiest of the three summit-block lines — a step down from the Classic Route and well below The Roof.

Roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft of gain, mostly on climbers' path and talus once past Snow Lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ALONG THE FOOT OF THE HORN: THE ROOF, THE CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK. OPEN BOOK IS THE RIGHTMOST AND THE EASIEST.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS UNMISTAKABLE AND IT IS A COUNT: TWO WIDE, LEFT-LEANING CRACKS, ABOUT 50 FT RIGHT OF THE CLASSIC ROUTE'S BASE. Two of them, wide, leaning left. From there the line climbs up and LEFT toward the anchor shared with the other routes.

THE NEGATIVE IS ABOUT CRACK WIDTH AND YOU FEEL IT IN THE FIRST FEW MOVES, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHEN YOU WANT TO KNOW: IF THE CRACK TAKES YOUR FINGERS AND HANDS COMFORTABLY, YOU ARE ON THE CLASSIC ROUTE, 50 FT TO YOUR LEFT, AT 5.4. Open Book's cracks are wide and awkward and want large cams — that awkwardness is the route, not a sign you are off it.

THE SECOND NEGATIVE IS OVERHEAD: IF THERE IS A ROOF ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE WALKED THE ENTIRE WIDTH OF THE BLOCK AND YOU ARE ON THE ROOF AT 5.6 — the hardest of the three and the far left end of the list.

ORIENTATION TEST: this line is on the EAST-FACING side of the pinnacle. The Classic Route goes straight up the SOUTH face. If you are directly beneath the south face looking up at blocky ground with a piton visible at half height, you are one line to the left of here.

DESCENT: the same shared anchor as the other two — the large rock horn on the south side, about 40-50 ft above the notch. AVOID THE OLD DEAD SNAG some older reports mention; it is no longer trustworthy. A 30 m rope has been found marginal or short depending on which of the two rappel lines you take off the horn, so 40 m removes the doubt. Downclimbing this line is viable given the grade, but it is still exposed near the top.
hazards: Wide-crack climbing that is awkward and poorly protected without large cams
Loose rock in the gully and chimney terrain around the summit tower
Loose talus and scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out
An exposed step near the top of the horn with real air below on the east side
A 30 m rope that may not reach on one of the two rappel lines

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the leftmost line on the summit horn
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as the other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, the maintained trail about a mile and roughly 700 ft to Snow Lake for the last reliable water. Past the lake the tread fades over a wooded hump; contour up and right into the obvious northwest talus and dirt gully, where a heather-bench climbers' path reappears near the top and drops you into the basin under the peak. Climb the moraine beside the small basin snowfield to Unicorn Col, then follow the traversing use trail below the summit cliffs on the south side to the base of the horn — roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way and about 2,400 ft of gain.

This is the hardest and most exposed of the three summit-block lines, following a steeper and more sustained line than either neighbour, with an old piton at about half height.

Carry a double-length runner or a cordelette. The top anchor for this line sits set back from the edge, so the rappel power-point has to be extended out to the lip to keep the rope running cleanly over the roof feature.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ALONG THE FOOT OF THE HORN: THE ROOF, THE CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK. THE ROOF IS THE LEFTMOST AND THE HARDEST.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A JUNCTION RATHER THAN A CRACK, WHICH IS WHY IT IS EASY TO FIND IN POOR LIGHT: IT STARTS ABOUT 20 FT LEFT OF THE CLASSIC ROUTE, AT THE POINT WHERE THE RIDGELINE MEETS THE SUMMIT BLOCK. Ridge into block — that meeting point is the marker.

THE FEATURE ITSELF IS THE SECOND CONFIRMATION AND IT IS OVERHEAD: A WIDE GULLY OR CHIMNEY RUNNING BENEATH A ROOF. You climb the gully, then STEP RIGHT UNDER THE ROOF onto a ledge, then up to the belay. IF THERE IS NO ROOF ABOVE YOU, YOU ARE NOT ON THIS ROUTE. There is an old piton at about half height.

THE TWO NEGATIVES, BOTH TO YOUR RIGHT:
  — 20 FT RIGHT, blocky climbing straight up the open south face with a piton mid-pitch, and no roof: that is the CLASSIC ROUTE at 5.4.
  — 70 FT RIGHT, two wide left-leaning cracks: that is OPEN BOOK at easy fifth.
So every way of being wrong here makes the climbing EASIER, not harder — which is the safer direction, but it also means nothing about the ground will warn you that you missed the route you came for.

GRADE AS A CHECK: 5.6, noticeably burlier than the Classic Route's corner and well above Open Book. If it feels like the easiest thing on the block, you are not on it.

AND THE ONE PIECE OF DESCENT PLANNING THAT HAS TO HAPPEN BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE GROUND: the top anchor for this line is SET BACK FROM THE EDGE. Extend it with a cordelette or long sling so the rope runs over the lip rather than dragging on the roof. Most parties rappel this line even if they downclimbed elsewhere on the peak, because reversing it is considerably more exposed than reversing its neighbours. A single-rope rappel of roughly 40-50 ft; 30 m has been reported marginal depending on which of the two lines off the horn you use, so 40 m removes the guesswork. Use the rock horn, not the retired snag.
hazards: Loose rock reported in the gully and chimney section
The steepest and most exposed of the three summit-block lines, and awkward to reverse
A top anchor set back from the edge, which drags the rope over the roof unless extended
An old piton at half height that should not be treated as protection
A 30 m rope that may not reach on one of the two rappel lines

approach_variants.name: Bench Lake and Snow Lake into the Unicorn Creek cirque, beneath the northwest face
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-Mar, and only in a year when it forms at all
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Stevens Canyon Road to the Bench Lake and Snow Lake trailhead, on the south side of the road about 1.5 miles east of the Reflection Lakes parking area. From the trailhead near 4,550 ft, follow the trail 0.75 mile to Bench Lake, then a further half mile to Snow Lake at 4,685 ft, which sits in a glacial cirque directly below the peak.

From the lake, continue up the Unicorn Creek drainage south and east into the upper cirque to the base of the northwest face. Roughly 1.5 to 2 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain from the car to the base of the ice.

In winter, when Stevens Canyon Road is gated, add about 3 miles of unplowed road from Narada Falls; one spring party on skis reported four hours from the car to the base of the climbing.

There are no fixed anchors on the face. Retreat means threads you build.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS ON THE OPPOSITE SIDE OF THE PEAK FROM EVERY OTHER ROUTE HERE, AND THAT IS THE FIRST AND CLEAREST FINDING. The summit-block lines are approached round to the SOUTH side via Unicorn Col. THIS ONE CLIMBS THE NORTHWEST FACE DIRECTLY OUT OF THE SNOW LAKE CIRQUE — you never go to the col at all. If you are traversing under cliffs on the south side of the peak, you are on the wrong side of the mountain for this climb.

THE APPROACH IS COUNTABLE AND ENTIRELY ON KNOWN GROUND: Bench Lake at about 0.75 mile, Snow Lake at 4,685 ft at about 1.25 miles, then up the Unicorn Creek drainage south and east into the upper cirque. SNOW LAKE SITS DIRECTLY BELOW THE FACE — the wall you are looking at from the lake is the wall you climb. There is no second cirque to confuse it with.

THE STRONGEST TEST IS THE ICE ITSELF, AND IT IS A GO OR NO-GO RATHER THAN A NAVIGATION AID: PITCH ONE IS SUSTAINED VERTICAL ICE. IF WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU IS 50-DEGREE SNOW, EITHER YOU ARE NOT AT THE ROUTE OR IT HAS NOT FORMED THIS YEAR. This climb does not always form, and there is nothing fixed to rappel off if you go up and find that out at half height.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE CONFIRMS IT, IN ORDER: vertical ice, then about 50-degree ice, then steep rime and choss to the summit. If the climbing eases early and STAYS eased, you are on a snow line and not on this.

AND THE THING THAT MAKES THIS COMMITTING RATHER THAN MERELY HARD: IT FINISHES ON THE SUMMIT. There is no walk-off from the top of the face. You rappel the summit block — about 50 ft, off the slung block on the south side rather than the retired snag — then downclimb the class 3 south slope and ridge WEST to the col at about 6,605 ft between Unicorn and West Unicorn, drop north into the basin, and follow it back to Snow Lake. In winter that descent is a serious undertaking on its own: the basin and gully are avalanche terrain, the col can be corniced, and you will likely be doing it in fading light. Know that ground before you start up it in the dark.
hazards: The route does not form every year, and there are no fixed anchors on the face — retreat means V-threads
Rime and choss on the upper pitch
A committing descent off the summit in winter, through avalanche terrain in the basin and gully, often in fading light
A corniced col on the descent between Unicorn and West Unicorn
A cold, exposed northwest aspect with a long unplowed road walk when the highway is gated

_SKIPPED.wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish: DUPLICATE ROW. This and wa_mount_rainier_liberty_ridge describe the same climb — Liberty Ridge, from White River over St Elmo Pass to the Carbon, finishing at Liberty Cap. Same high point (14,112 ft), gain within 8 ft of each other (9,700 vs 9,708), same trailhead, same first ascent party in 1935. Liberty Ridge has no variant that stops anywhere but Liberty Cap, so there is no second climb here for a second row to describe. The Rainier-filed row ALREADY CARRIES a variant with a base finding ('the base is the toe of the ridge on the Carbon Glacier, and the whole approach is a sequence of things you must leave'), and writing a second one would put two approaches and two base findings on one climb. See _DEFECTS.
_SKIPPED.wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish: DUPLICATE ROW, same shape as the one above. This and wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge both describe Ptarmigan Ridge finishing at Liberty Cap, same 14,112 ft high point, same 1935 first ascent by Bauer and Hossack. The Rainier-filed row already carries TWO variants — one from Mowich Lake and Spray Park, one from White River via St Elmo Pass — which are exactly the two approaches this row's own prose names. Nothing is left to say that is not already said on a row a climber is more likely to open. See _DEFECTS.
_SKIPPED.wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder: DUPLICATE ROW. This and wa_frying_pan_whitman_glaciers are the same climb under two names — Little Tahoma's standard line, which guidebooks call the East Shoulder AND the Fryingpan/Whitman Glaciers route. The rows agree on every measurable field: same first ascent (Flett and Garrison, 29 August 1894), same gain (7,600 ft), same distance (11.3 km), same grade, same season string, same hazards array, same two-entry pitch_detail. wa_frying_pan_whitman_glaciers carries a far longer approach with the cliff-out trap above Summerland and the Whitman Notch elevation, so that is the row written. See _DEFECTS.
_SKIPPED.wa_mount_adams_northwest_ridge: POSITIONED ONLY RELATIVE TO ITS NEIGHBOUR. The entire approach on this row is one sentence: 'Same approach as the standard North Ridge route, via the Killen Creek Trail and PCT.' Its beta then describes 'the northwest face of the North Ridge' — which is the feature adams_northwest_ridge ('North Face of the Northwest Ridge') already describes, from the same camp, with the same aspect. There is no independent marker anywhere in the row: no bergschrund, no constriction, no named rock, no elevation at which anything happens. Its five pitches of AI1-2 could be told from its neighbour's three by counting rope lengths, but that is a test you can only apply once you are committed, which is the opposite of a base finding.
